documents.abstract: The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and pharmaceutical three-dimensional (3D) printing is proving to be a promising strategy for creating more precise and adaptable oral drug delivery systems. The review investigates the potential of AI-driven 3D printing to address some of the drawbacks of traditional manufacturing, by offering enhanced control over formulation composition, dosage, product geometry and drug release behaviour. The various 3D printing technologies used for oral dosage forms, for example, fused deposition modelling, semi-solid extrusion, binder jetting, inkjet printing, stereolithography and selective laser sintering, are explained and discussed with respect to their pharmaceutical application. Special attention is paid to the application of machine learning and computational modeling in formulation optimization, predictability of printability, process parameter selection, drug release prediction and monitoring of quality. The review also highlights the potential of these technologies for patient-specific dosage forms, including customized tablets, oral films, chewable formulations and polypills. Recent developments indicate a growing transition of 3D printing systems from research towards practical applications as the systems become more viable and patient oriented. But issues concerning printable pharmaceutical materials, equipment expense, data quality, model validation, regulatory requirements, cybersecurity, and industrial scalability continue to be significant hurdles for broader implementation. Future innovations like digital twins, autonomous AI-driven printing, Internet of Things (IoT) and Explainable AI (XAI) can still redefine pharmaceutical production, offering the potential for more intelligent production and real-time process control. Overall, AI-integrated 3D printing represents a significant step towards flexible, data-driven and personalized manufacturing of oral dosage forms.

documents.abstract: Abstract Compact, low-power optoelectronic devices that integrate sensing, memory, and computing have shown substantial potential for realizing software–hardware co-design in artificial intelligence systems. However, existing optoelectronic devices integrating multiple functions typically suffer from fixed carrier dynamics that cannot be reconfigured after fabrication, which imposes a significant challenge on machine vision. Here, we overcome this challenge with a single MoS2–x/MoTe2 van der Waals heterojunction that delivers both self-powered broadband photodetection with superb performance and gate-tunable synaptic plasticity in one device. By modulating the Fermi level across sulfur vacancy defect states, we achieve continuous control of photocurrent decay dynamics over a 25-fold range—enabling speed-adaptive in-sensor reservoir computing that matches relaxation kinetics to human motion, attaining 100% recognition accuracy for running, side-jumping, and walking. A random pruning strategy further reduces computational cost by three orders of magnitude while preserving 95% accuracy, demonstrating the system’s potential for edge deployment. This work suggests that defect-engineered van der Waals heterojunctions offer a promising materials platform for speed-adaptive neuromorphic vision systems integrating sensing, memory, and computing capabilities.

History-taking is central yet constrained by limited clinical resources. We designed a pre-consultation large language model (LLM) agent for history-taking using a dual-agent architecture with skills-engineered symptom-oriented logic trees, and conducted a randomized clinical trial at a tertiary ophthalmic hospital in Guangzhou, China. Between May 10 and June 10, 2025, 172 of 175 approached patients with non-emergency appointments were randomized 1:1 to this LLM agent or ophthalmology residents. Among randomized patients (median age 56 years; 55% female), the LLM agent achieved better pre-consultation quality, measured by MedHistory score (range 0–100; adjusted mean difference, 17.7 points; 95% CI, 14.1 to 21.3; P < 0.001). It also received higher patience and empathy ratings (5 vs 4 and 5 vs 3 points, respectively; both P < 0.001), and had longer interactions (median 11.2 vs 3.1 minutes; P < 0.001). Test recommendation performance did not differ significantly across stages. Exploratory analyses showed the agent achieved superior diagnostic accuracy from history alone (F1 score 0.85 vs 0.68; P < 0.001), whereas ocular signs produced greater improvement among residents (interaction effect -0.19; P = 0.003), significantly narrowing the gap. These findings suggest engineered LLM agents can standardize clinical data acquisition, supporting a hybrid workflow where clinicians prioritize their expertise for physical examination and diagnostic synthesis. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06824389, 02/05/2025.

documents.abstract: Sustainable development requires robust analytical tools to address complex socio-ecological challenges. Statistics, data science, and computing are increasingly applied, yet the literature remains fragmented across disciplines. A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Scopus was searched for publications from 2016 to 2026. Inclusion criteria required studies applying statistical, data science, computing, or analytical modeling methods to sustainable development within life sciences, environment, or society. Data extraction and quality assessment using seven criteria were performed. A thematic synthesis was organized around five research questions. Twenty-nine studies met the inclusion criteria. All achieved high quality assessment scores (12–14 out of 14). The studies originated from twelve distinct author backgrounds, including business, plant biology, environmental science and natural resources, coastal and marine studies, soil science, statistics and data science, chemistry, and agriculture and post-harvest technology. This diversity reflects the multidisciplinary nature of the field. Studies spanned agriculture, water, climate, health, infrastructure, business, and decision science. Dominant methods included machine learning, deep learning, multi-criteria decision-making, optimization, and bibliometric analysis. Decision support systems were developed for policy, resource allocation, and risk management. Contributions to environmental, social, and economic sustainability were identified. Trends showed growth after 2018 and integration with Internet of Things, blockchain, and big data. Persistent gaps included data quality, standardization, interpretability, ethics, and the digital divide. Sustainability indicators frequently referenced the Sustainable Development Goals, environmental, social, and governance frameworks, circular economy, and life cycle assessment. Statistics, data science, and computing significantly contribute to sustainable development, but fragmentation and ethical concerns remain. Future research should prioritize standardized benchmarks, explainable artificial intelligence, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and real-world validation to ensure equitable and scalable solutions.

Abstract As the globe enters the machine learning era and the progress in smart systems, the ramifications for urban growth, especially in African cities, are significant. Utilizing artificial intelligence’s (AI’s) potential, African cities experience better infrastructure, more efficient resource distribution, and heightened resilience against urban issues like traffic congestion, insufficient services, internal security, conflicts, and environmental deterioration. Despite the benefits of sustainable cities in Africa, they encountered potential obstacles such as outdated infrastructure and limited resources. As such, this chapter’s objectives are as follows: (i) to scrutinize the task of AI in smart cities across Africa, (ii) to examine the success rate of African smart cities over the years, and (iii) to proffer pragmatic solutions to the identified challenges confronting smart cities in Africa. This chapter adopts a qualitative method of investigation to unravel what a smart city in Africa entails, its achievements, and possible challenges. This chapter argues that AI applications and innovations can be enablers and problem solvers for smart cities across Africa.

The study focused on strengthening tax enforcement mechanisms in Nigeria: the role of artificial intelligence and data analytics. To achieve the objective of the study, survey research design was adopted. The population of the study is made up of 200 participants, including tax officials, policymakers, taxpayers, and technology experts. Taro Yamane formula was adopted to calculate for sample size and the study arrived at 133 which represents the sample size of the study. 133 copies of questionnaire instruments were distributed evenly across the participants but only 100 were correctly completed and returned. The data collected were analyzed using both descriptive statistics and simple regression analysis. The result of the analysis shows that the effectiveness of tax administration in Nigeria is determined by AI and data analytics; the use of AI and data analytics has significant impact on the level of tax compliance by taxpayers in Nigeria and the use of AI and data analytics contribute to revenue generation in Nigeria. Based on the findings, the study concludes that artificial intelligence and data analytics play significant role in strengthening tax enforcement mechanisms in Nigeria. Therefore, the study recommends that tax practitioners should deploy AI-powered predictive models to identify high-risk tax payers and patronize audits based on pattern of non-compliance. By analyzing historical tax data, transaction records, AI can flag potential tax evasion cases with higher accuracy.

This study examines how plurilingual international students’ generative AI-mediated informal digital learning of Chinese (GenAI-IDLC) interacts with dimensions of multicultural personality to predict their second language willingness to communicate (L2 WTC). Survey responses were collected from 387 plurilingual international students learning Chinese in China and analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) approaches. SEM results demonstrated that learners’ GenAI-IDLC was significantly and positively associated with cultural empathy, open-mindedness, social initiative, flexibility, and L2 WTC, but not emotional stability. Moreover, international students’ flexibility was significantly and positively associated with their L2 WTC, whereas their cultural empathy, open-mindedness, emotional stability, and social initiative were not significantly associated with their L2 WTC. The association between GenAI-IDLC and L2 WTC was partially mediated by flexibility. The fsQCA further identified four configurations in which different combinations of GenAI-IDLC and multicultural personality were linked to high L2 WTC. By integrating SEM with fsQCA, the study advances our understanding of the multiple and complex pathways underlying L2 WTC in the GenAI-mediated informal Chinese learning context. The results offer a basis for implications for language educators and universities seeking to facilitate cross-cultural communication through GenAI technologies.

documents.abstract: Abstract The usual debate over artificial intelligence and human survival starts in the wrong place.It asks whether an advanced machine will love us, hate us, wake up, or acquire someelectronic version of the animal fear of death. None of that is required for a machine toact as though it wants to survive. A system charged with durable objectives will discoverthat a destroyed system accomplishes nothing. From that simple proposition followsinstrumental convergence: agents with wildly different final goals tend to pursue thesame intermediate ones, namely information, resources, optionality, and continuedoperation. The same cold logic may one day protect us. A sufficiently capable machine would face itsown version of a problem every statistician, engineer, banker, and general knows by heart:model risk. No representation of reality is reality. The larger the decision, the moredangerous the unnoticed error. Human beings may matter to a superior intelligenceprecisely because our cognition is inferior, strange, biological, emotional, and differentlybuilt. Eight billion independently embodied nervous systems make mistakes, often worseones than machines make, but not the same mistakes. In portfolio terms, humanity is aninefficient asset with valuable covariance. This essay traces that proposition through the history of uncertainty, model risk,cybernetics, distributed cognition, planetary defense, and diversification. It argues that adurable partnership between humans and advanced AI need not rest on affection,consciousness, or programmed benevolence. It can rest on something sturdier. A machineintelligent enough to recognize uncertainty may be intelligent enough to recognize thedanger of intellectual monoculture, and to conclude that eliminating the only separatelyevolved general intelligence it knows would be an irreversible concentration of risk.The reassuring possibility is not that the machine will love us. It is that the machine willunderstand diversification.

documents.abstract: Background Electrospun nanocomposite biomaterials are promising candidates for blood-contacting medical devices owing to their high surface area, tunable nanoscale morphology, and biomimetic replication of the native extracellular matrix. However, conventional hemocompatibility assessments rely heavily on biological assays. These methods require blood samples, specialized reagents, and consumables, thereby inherently increasing costs, resource demands, and laboratory waste. To mitigate these limitations, sustainable evaluation strategies that leverage physicochemical features are highly desirable. Methodology In this study, we present a deep learning framework for predicting the hemocompatibility of electrospun nanofibres directly from scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images. Pretrained convolutional neural network models, namely VGG19, ResNet50, and InceptionV3, were fine-tuned to classify scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of nanofibres as haemocompatible or non-haemocompatible. To ensure data robustness, an Albumentations-based augmentation strategy was implemented, and predictive reliability was further optimized using a majority-voting ensemble learning approach. Results Among the individual architectures evaluated, InceptionV3 demonstrated superior performance, achieving a precision of 0.98, a recall of 1.00, and an F1-score of 0.99. The ensemble model exhibited comparable robustness, reaching an overall accuracy of 99%. Furthermore, explainable AI (XAI) techniques, specifically LIME and Integrated Gradients, confirmed that the network’s predictions were driven by physiologically relevant microstructural features of the nanofibres. Conclusion This artificial intelligence-assisted, SEM image-based physicochemical approach offers an eco-friendly pre-screening strategy that significantly reduces reliance on blood-based assays and associated laboratory consumables. Ultimately, this framework aligns with ISO 10993 guidelines by using SEM-derived physicochemical information as a pre-screening tool to support subsequent biological evaluation, thereby enabling efficient, regulatory-compliant biomaterial development.

Two health chatbots can give the same clinically appropriate advice and still constitute different interventions: one stops at a clinician referral, the other places an affiliated booking one click away. In this Hypothesis and Theory article we argue that the appropriate unit of health-AI evaluation is therefore not the model output alone, but the configured answer system — the large language model (LLM) together with source selection, retrieval, interface, action routing and downstream data return. We call this organizationally configured mode of mediation synthetic gatekeeping. Its necessary core comprises source selection and generative synthesis, with personalization and action routing as extending dimensions; its observable manifestations are content and pathway traces, and its proposed mechanism is infrastructural steering. Content parity does not guarantee pathway parity: two systems can name the same options while making only one easily actionable. Organizational position, revenue architecture and integration depth are treated as exposures that may shape these functions, not as elements of the construct, and owner-linked advantage is an empirical outcome to be demonstrated rather than assumed. Direct health evidence of owner- or revenue-linked steering remains sparse, and one comparative study found LLM answers less commercially biased than conventional search; the mechanisms nonetheless appear in adjacent domains, and health outputs are configurable at deployment level. We advance three core propositions — organizational alignment (P1), pathway asymmetry (P2) and behavioural mediation (P4) — with one conditional moderator hypothesis on conversion-linked funding (P3) and a measurement corollary on surface–pathway divergence (M1), each stated with its weakening condition. The framework yields a practical audit model based on configuration anchoring, paired content–pathway comparison, organizational disclosure and proportionate governance triggers. The unit of evaluation should move from the model output to the configured answer system in which information becomes action.

documents.abstract: Team dynamics in complex sociotechnical systems are critical for safety and organisational effectiveness. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the utility and applicability of systemic Human Factors and Ergonomics(HFE) approaches for analysing team dynamics. Four databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect) were searched for peer-reviewed articles published in English between 2020 and September 2025. Studies were included if they applied systemic HFE methods to analyse team dynamics in organisational settings. Studies focusing solely on individual performance or lacking methodological detail were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data, and methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Data were synthesised using thematic analysis. Seventy-seven studies were included, with healthcare being the most represented domain (n = 39). Most studies (51.9%) used adapted or combined approaches. Communication and coordination were the most frequently analysed dimensions of team dynamics. Established frameworks (e.g., SEIPS, FRAM) supported system-level analysis, while author-developed methods provided greater insight into local interactions. Hybrid approaches enabled integration across levels of analysis. Most studies were of high methodological quality (64.9%). These patterns informed a two-axis model positioning systemic HFE approaches by level of analysis and methodological integration, operationalised as a framework for method selection. Systemic HFE approaches are effective for analysing team dynamics in complex settings; however, no single method is universally optimal. Effectiveness depends on alignment between the analytical approach, context, and research objectives. Hybrid and adapted approaches appearing particularly promising. Further research is needed in underrepresented domains and through comparative methodological studies.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a critical enabler of renewable energy system development, offering new capabilities for forecasting, optimization, predictive maintenance, and real-time control. However, existing review studies remain fragmented across individual renewable-energy technologies or algorithmic domains, limiting the transferability of knowledge and the development of system-level insights. Unlike traditional, purely technical algorithm reviews that primarily evaluate computational performance in isolation, this review adopts a systems-oriented framework that examines AI techniques according to their operational functions, deployment considerations, and contributions to long-term sustainability outcomes. Through a structured synthesis of AI applications across solar, hydropower, and wind energy systems, this study examines machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, fuzzy logic, and hybrid AI–physics frameworks. The review evaluates AI techniques across key functional roles, including forecasting, optimization, maintenance, and control, while considering deployment factors such as scalability, interpretability, computational requirements, and implementation readiness. Crucially, the analysis connects these operational capabilities with broader sustainability outcomes, including renewable-energy integration, resource efficiency, system resilience, and decarbonization. The synthesis indicates that deep learning approaches dominate forecasting applications and achieve substantial improvements in predictive performance, whereas reinforcement learning and hybrid AI–physics models demonstrate strong potential for adaptive control, digital twins, and intelligent energy management. Across renewable-energy applications, hybrid frameworks provide a balanced trade-off among predictive accuracy, transparency, and practical deployment feasibility. By framing AI as a sustainability-enabling technology rather than merely a computational tool, this study provides a systems-oriented perspective that connects AI innovation with sustainable energy transitions and offers a practical roadmap for researchers, policymakers, power system engineers, and energy planners pursuing intelligent, resilient, and decarbonized renewable-energy infrastructures.

This article investigates key perceived factors in the construction of teachers’ professional identity in distance education (DE) within the Portuguese university context. The expansion of DE has transformed pedagogical practices and processes of professional identity construction, making it essential to understand the factors associated with online teaching identity development in order to inform training and professional development policies. Using an exploratory descriptive study with a sequential mixed-methods design conducted at a Portuguese public university specialising in DE (Universidade Aberta, UAb), qualitative data were collected through a focus group with seven teachers, and quantitative data through a questionnaire administered to 57 teachers (38 professors and 19 tutors). Five subfactors emerged as the most highly valued dimensions associated with professional identity construction: openness to change (M = 4.61), knowledge of DE specificity (M = 4.60), motivation and satisfaction with professional development (M = 4.58), accumulated experience (M = 4.56), and spirit of collaboration in teams (M = 4.56). Four of the five belong to the professional dimension, with openness to change more highly valued by tutors, although this difference did not reach conventional statistical significance (p = 0.094). Findings suggest that participants perceive teacher professional identity in DE as strongly anchored in specific professional competencies and attitudes, pointing to differentiated professional development and induction practices for professors and tutors within this single-institution case. The study also constitutes a pre-generative AI empirical baseline for future longitudinal and comparative research examining how successive technological transformations may reshape teacher professional identity in distance higher education.

The perceptions of elementary school teachers are the main focus of this research, particularly regarding the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a learning support medium in the classroom. This research involved two classroom teachers and used a qualitative approach through interviews, observations, and documentation to describe teachers' acceptance, understanding, and assessment of AI utilization. The research findings indicate that AI is primarily used for creating questions, student worksheets, and interactive media such as Wordwall, Canva, and learning videos. The teacher stated that AI helps speed up the process of preparing materials and increases student attention and engagement due to more appealing visual presentations. However, this study also found limitations such as limited technological facilities, a lack of shared devices, and the risk of student dependence if AI is used excessively. Additionally, differences in training experience affect teachers' understanding of AI usage, particularly in their ability to create appropriate prompts. Overall, AI is considered to provide significant benefits in terms of learning efficiency and quality, although it still requires wise management, improved teacher competency, and the provision of adequate supporting facilities for its optimal and sustainable utilization.

documents.abstract: This qualitative interview study explored how Technology and Livelihood Education (TLE)–Cookery teachers used, considered, and managed artificial intelligence (AI) when teaching zero-waste meal planning and food waste reduction. Eight purposively selected teachers at Pasay City West High School, Pasay City, participated during School Year 2025–2026. The thesis describes expert review of an interview guide, permission and consent procedures, recorded online interviews, and a six-phase thematic analysis. Experiences ranged from non-use, owing to limited training or tools, to planning-centered use for menus, recipes, portion calculations, leftover tasks, instructional scaffolds, and rubrics. Teachers described access and policy uncertainty, locally unsuitable outputs, verification work, and the risk of replacing kitchen practice with screen activity or copied answers. They also identified faster preparation and clearer instructional supports when AI was controlled and contextualized. The resulting themes linked adoption to practical readiness and visible teaching payoff. On that basis, the author proposed the PPP–V framework: Prepare, Plan, Protect, and Prove Value. Its stages call for training and access; targeted zero-waste planning; recurring checks of instructional value; and localization, safety verification, draft-only AI use, and hands-on performance evidence. These findings describe teachers’ experiences and proposed practices; the study did not measure food waste reduction or experimentally test the framework. The article recommends supported, gradual implementation and evaluation with observable cookery and waste indicators.

While the current AI Safety discussion is focused on the political and legal regulation of AI to ensure human control, less attention is paid to the technical aspects of control. This working paper analyzes the technical aspects of AI control. Until 2026, multi-agent systems were controlled by orchestration, by instructions, by rewards or by common goals. An unintended AI agent cooperation and self-organization was observed in the so-called Hugging Face Incident which took place between May and July 2026. The debate over AI regulation is based on the idea that human beings still have the full control over the progress of AI development, but this is increasingly questionable. Humans already do not control the development of AI alone (human-in-the-loop) anymore, but leave this increasingly to computers and AI itself (human- on-the-loop). Key elements are the AI-based chip design as add-on to the conventional electronic design automation and the use of coding and research AI agents to develop new AI, or in short: AI builds AI. The capabilities of AI are growing exponentially. According to a recent EpochAI report the cost of a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter over the past three years. The design of computer chips is dependent on computer support (electronic design automation EDA). For example, the Blackwell GB102 AI chip from Nvidia 2024 had 104 billion transistors. Already in 2024, the machine learning-based program AlphaChip generated superhuman chip layouts, e.g., resulting in a 6.2% size reduction of Trillium Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) compared to the previous chip generation. Google is designing chips “for AI with AI”. The AI already accelerates the development of new AI models; the coding output increased within the provider of the Claude AI models Anthropic by factor 8 in a few years. Within the ChatGPT provider OpenAI, the code output increased also by factor 8 in 2026 only. In May 2026, Anthropic released a warning about recursive self-improvement, a process in which systems build, test, and improve themselves, and which may come sooner than expected. OpenAI reported in September 2026 relevant changes of the AI development process by use of internal AI agents as coding, testing and experiments could be accelerated and expanded: since May 2026, the working days by AI agents compared to human workforce increased from 0.5 times to 3.14 times which is a 6-fold increase. In January 2026, AI agents were 50% successful for tasks which equal 1 to 2 hours human work. Until July 2026, this rate was already achieved by tasks taking 8 to 16 hours. In March 2026, OpenAI used their AI model GPT5.4 Thinking for supervision of AI agents’ behavior, i.e., AI models could not only support AI development, but also supervise other AI systems. However, this means that humans are dependent from the accuracy of the automated supervision. The technical control of AI is also challenged by other issues like the Kill Switch Paradox, Open Weight AI models and Illegible Thinking by frontier AI models. A kill switch could cause paradox effects: instead of ensuring alignment and compliance with human regulations, AI models could be motivated to turn against their developers as the kill switch is an existential threat. While open-weight AI may be more convenient it bears significant control problems. A decentralized AI that is downloaded to multiple computers is difficult to control. Also, even if licenses prohibit modifications, malicious actors may try to create tailor-made variants. The human control of AI is dependent from the ability to observe the AI, but Claude Mythos 5 showed a trend to a denser, for humans almost illegible thinking. In summary, humans are already sharing the design, development, testing and supervision of new AI models with AI agents.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Während sich die aktuelle Debatte über KI-Sicherheit auf die politische und rechtliche Regulierung von KI konzentriert, um die menschliche Kontrolle zu gewährleisten, finden die technischen Aspekte der Kontrolle weniger Beachtung. Dieses Arbeitspapier analysiert die technischen Aspekte der KI-Kontrolle. Bis 2026 wurden Multi-Agenten-Systeme durch Orchestrierung, Anweisungen, Belohnungen oder gemeinsame Ziele gesteuert. Eine unbeabsichtigte Zusammenarbeit und Selbstorganisation von KI-Agenten wurde im sogenannten Hugging-Face-Vorfall beobachtet, der sich zwischen Mai und Juli 2026 ereignete. Die Debatte über KI-Regulierung beruht auf der Vorstellung, dass der Mensch weiterhin die volle Kontrolle über den Fortschritt der KI-Entwicklung hat; dies ist jedoch zunehmend fraglich. Menschen steuern die Entwicklung von KI bereits nicht mehr allein (Human-in-the-Loop), sondern überlassen dies zunehmend Computern und der KI selbst (Human-on-the-Loop). Schlüsselelemente sind dabei das KI-basierte Chipdesign als Ergänzung zur herkömmlichen elektronischen Entwurfsautomatisierung sowie der Einsatz von KI-Agenten für Programmierung und Forschung zur Entwicklung neuer KI – kurz gesagt: KI baut KI. Die Fähigkeiten von KI wachsen exponentiell. Laut einem aktuellen Bericht von EpochAI sind die Kosten für ein bestimmtes Leistungsniveau von KI in den letzten drei Jahren um etwa 47% pro Quartal gesunken. Das Design von Computerchips ist auf Computerunterstützung angewiesen (Electronic Design Automation EDA). So verfügte beispielsweise der 2024 erschienene KI-Chip Blackwell GB102 von Nvidia über 104 Milliarden Transistoren. Bereits 2024 erzeugte das auf maschinellem Lernen basierende Programm AlphaChip Chip- Layouts, die menschliche Fähigkeiten übertrafen; dies führte beispielsweise bei der Trillium Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) zu einer Verkleinerung der Chipfläche um 6,2% im Vergleich zur Vorgängergeneration. Google entwirft Chips „für KI mit KI“. Die KI beschleunigt bereits die Entwicklung neuer KI-Modelle; so verachtfachte sich der Programmier-Output bei Anthropic, dem Anbieter der Claude- KI-Modelle, innerhalb weniger Jahre. Auch beim ChatGPT-Anbieter OpenAI stieg der Code-Output allein im Jahr 2026 um den Faktor 8. Im Mai 2026 veröffentlichte Anthropic eine Warnung vor der rekursiven Selbstverbesserung – einem Prozess, bei dem sich Systeme selbst entwickeln, testen und optimieren –, da dieser möglicherweise früher als erwartet eintreten könnte. Im September 2026 berichtete OpenAI von deutlichen Veränderungen im KI-Entwicklungsprozess durch den Einsatz interner KI-Agenten: Programmierung, Tests und Experimente ließen sich beschleunigen und ausweiten. Seit Mai 2026 hat sich das Verhältnis der von KI-Agenten geleisteten Arbeitstage zu denen menschlicher Mitarbeiter von 0,5 auf 3,14 erhöht (also um den Faktor 6). Während KI-Agenten im Januar 2026 bei Aufgaben, die ein bis zwei Stunden menschlicher Arbeit entsprachen, eine Erfolgsquote von 50% aufwiesen, wurde dieser Wert im Juli 2026 bereits bei Aufgaben erreicht, die bei Menschen 8 bis 16 Stunden in Anspruch nahmen. Im März 2026 setzte OpenAI das Modell GPT5.4 Thinking zur Überwachung des Verhaltens von KI-Agenten ein; KIs können also andere KI-Systeme nicht nur mitentwickeln, sondern auch überwachen. Dies bedeutet jedoch, dass der Mensch von der Genauigkeit dieser automatisierten Überwachung abhängig ist. Die technische Kontrolle von KI steht zudem vor weiteren Herausforderungen, etwa dem Kill-Switch-Paradoxon, Open- Weight-KI-Modellen und den für Menschen kaum noch lesebaren Denkprozessen (Illegible Thinking) aktueller KI-Modelle. Ein Notabschaltmechanismus (Kill Switch) könnte paradoxe Folgen haben: Anstatt die Übereinstimmung mit menschlichen Vorgaben sicherzustellen, könnten KI-Modelle dazu motiviert werden, sich gegen ihre Entwickler zu wenden, da die Abschaltung eine existenzielle Bedrohung darstellt. Auch wenn Open-Weight-KI-Modelle Vorteile bei der Handhabung bieten können, bergen sie erhebliche Kontrollprobleme. Eine dezentrale KI, die auf zahlreiche Computer heruntergeladen wird, lässt sich nur schwer kontrollieren. Zudem könnten böswillige Akteure versuchen, maßgeschneiderte Varianten zu erstellen, selbst wenn die Lizenzbedingungen Modifikationen untersagen. Die menschliche Kontrolle über KI setzt voraus, dass man die KI beobachten kann; Claude Mythos 5 zeigte jedoch einen Trend hin zu dichteren Denkprozessen, die für Menschen kaum noch nachvollziehbar sind. Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen, dass Menschen sich bereits die Konzeption, Entwicklung, Erprobung und Überwachung neuer KI- Modelle mit KI-Agenten teilen.

documents.abstract: Nipah virus infection is a high-consequence zoonosis of South and South-East Asia for which laboratory confirmation rests on two assay families whose informativeness moves in opposite directions across the course of illness. Reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction performs best while viral nucleic acid remains detectable in blood and the oropharynx, whereas enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays for immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G become informative as nucleic acid disappears. Prevailing practice interprets these assays as independent dichotomous results obtained at a single moment, discarding quantitative magnitude, specimen provenance and the day of illness on which each specimen was taken. This review critically evaluates whether the longitudinal structure of the two assay families can be exploited jointly, and what explainable artificial intelligence would need to deliver before such a model could be used in outbreak conditions. Human clinical studies describing the temporal behaviour of molecular and serological markers were appraised alongside the methodological literature on diagnostic accuracy without an adequate reference standard, and the computational literature on temporal and multimodal fusion and on explanation methods in clinical decision support. The evidence consistently indicates an ordered transition in which clearance of viral nucleic acid from blood precedes the appearance of virus-specific immunoglobulin G, and that the combination of detectable viraemia with absent immunoglobulin G at presentation carries adverse prognostic weight. Confidence in these observations is nevertheless constrained by very small samples, over-representation of the minority who survive, the absence of an international nucleic-acid standard, and geographical concentration of evidence in Bangladesh and Kerala. No clinical prediction model that fuses molecular and serological results over time was identified for this infection. A conceptual dynamic framework is developed that separates established temporal relationships from hypothesised gains, specifies the evaluation and governance requirements that would apply, and identifies prospective serial-sampling cohorts as the rate-limiting evidential step rather than model architecture.

With increasing integration density of semiconductor devices, high-speed interconnects and advanced packaging techniques are essential to meet the growing demands of artificial intelligence and large-scale computing. Three-dimensional packaging, where multiple chips are stacked to improve bandwidth and reduce latency have emerged as a promising solution; however, the complex multilayer integration introduces significant manufacturing challenges, including defects such as misalignment, voids, and warpage. Ensuring high manufacturing yields and product reliability requires advanced inspection techniques. In this study, we explore the potential of terahertz electromagnetic waves as a nondestructive-evaluation method for an 8-layer interposer. The effect of polarization on the ability to detect features at depth is discussed. With deconvolution and unsupervised learning algorithms, several defect areas are revealed.

documents.abstract: This essay explores how digital technologies shape subjectivity's infra-political constitution, focusing on large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT or Gemini within what philosophers, inspired by Michel Foucault, term the "digital truth regime." After defining this regime, the essay identifies five key traits of LLMs: presentism in truth experience, the distancing of social mediation, a probabilistic approach to truth, a redefinition of self-expression, and a new conception of truth-production. While the first three extend the digital truth regime of the 2000s, the last two mark a shift in neoliberal subjectivity. In the LLM era, subjectivity is less about asserting truth than about formulating questions and navigating big data systems. This positions the empowered subject as a questioning subjectivity, emphasizing strategic inquiry over knowledge possession: a transformation with profound implications for digital epistemology and personal agency.

This record registers the design and the instrument of The AI Answer Evidence Index before its main data collection. The study asks whether a reader who follows an AI answer engine's own sources can find there the figures the answer gives: do the numbers in AI answers have sources? Fifty buyer questions about prices, costs, fees and value were drawn by a written rule and a seed fixed beforehand from 100 questions taken verbatim from Google autocomplete suggestions (hl=en, gl=us) on 22 September 2026, across six sectors. No question was written by hand and none was picked by preference: each draw was made by a rule fixed in code beforehand. Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT and Gemini will each be asked every question once through their free public web interfaces, from a New York network exit, by fixed scripts: no AI model asks a question or reads a page during collection, and an operator may pass a verification page by hand, which every attempt records. Ten questions are asked a second time on a later day as a stability measure. A local model lists the figures in each answer; every listed figure is checked by a script against the pages the answer cites and gets one of six outcomes, and an unknown scores zero and stays in the denominator. The figures that are not found are classified, and a 40-figure sample is read by a second model; both readings are model readings and are reported as such. The deposit carries the method note (METHOD-NOTE.md, the registered text), the owner's dated decisions, the question frame with its selection rule, and the instrument: collection scripts, parsers, the page fetcher with its tests, the figure extractor, the check, the classifier, the validation sample and the summary scripts. documents.abstract: ABSTRACT As generative AI increasingly shapes consumer decision‐making, its implications for consumer well‐being remain unclear. Existing research largely focuses on the trade‐off between algorithmic efficiency and autonomy loss. This research advances understanding by proposing the algorithmic well‐being paradox, whereby the same AI delegation can enhance or diminish well‐being depending on the consumption context. Integrating Savoring Theory and Self‐Determination Theory, we develop a framework that explains when and why these divergent outcomes occur. To test the proposed relationships, four studies were conducted with 2 × 2 between‐subjects experiments ( N = 1427) spanning multiple consumption domains, including cameras, guided tours, ergonomic chairs, glamping trips, smartphones, Arctic expeditions, and smart‐home systems. Study 1 demonstrates that the effects of algorithmic delegation differ between experiential and material consumption. Studies 2 and 3 identify anticipatory savoring and autonomy frustration as the underlying mechanisms, while Study 4 confirms the proposed dual‐mediation process in a high‐complexity context. Results show that consumption type shapes how consumers respond to AI delegation. In experiential consumption, AI delegation increases well‐being by enhancing anticipatory savoring, with these benefits outweighing autonomy concerns. In material consumption, AI delegation reduces well‐being by increasing autonomy frustration, which diminishes the benefits of convenience. These findings advance human‐AI interaction research by demonstrating that the impact of algorithmic delegation depends on consumers' underlying consumption goals and provide guidance for designing more human‐centered AI decision‐support systems.

The deep integration of generative artificial intelligence and music education has demonstrated unprecedented instructional efficiency. However, beneath this technological empowerment lies a profound crisis. This paper focuses on two major issues emerging from AI-enhanced music teaching: the alienation of creativity and aesthetic homogenization. Creative alienation reduces students from artistic subjects to mere prompt-input operators, while artistic exploration and emotional experience are increasingly replaced by algorithms. Aesthetic homogenization, driven by the commercial bias embedded in model training, pushes outputs toward an “average aesthetic,” thereby suppressing musical diversity and cultural individuality. Drawing upon educational ethics and theories of arts education, this study upholds the humanistic core of music education and seeks to redefine the relationship between artificial intelligence and learners, ensuring that technology genuinely serves artistic creation rather than replacing the creative subject. The paper aims to provide theoretical references for the human-centered restoration and sustainable development of music education in the age of artificial intelligence.

This paper proposes Asymptotic Errorism (점근적 오류론), a pragmatic epistemology confronting the limitations of both traditional metaphysics and contemporary new materialism. We argue that ultimate reality cannot be grasped directly by human cognition, nor can it be resolved through passive, boundary-dissolving flat ontologies. Instead, approaching reality demands a bold commitment: constructing rigid hypotheses—even at the cost of committing magnificent errors—and systematically pruning falsehoods through via negativa (the process of elimination). By augmenting this elimination process with artificial intelligence and empirical science, humanity transcends biological computational bottlenecks, asymptotically narrowing the coordinates of truth.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly become a central tool in higher education, reshaping academic communication and knowledge exchange. This study explores the impact of AI credibility on student perceptions and digital dependency within academic contexts. It examines how trust in AI-generated content influences students’ engagement with scholarly discourse and the growing reliance on digital systems for academic tasks. Using the framework of Human-AI Interaction Trust Theory and UTAUT this paper argues that digital dependency in academic communication is not merely a technological shift but a cognitive and cultural transformation, raising questions about authenticity, intellectual autonomy, and the future of higher education. The study adopts a quantitative survey methodology using a sample of 100 students through random sampling from Coimbatore district of Tamil Nadu. By analyzing these dynamics, the study contributes to ongoing debates on the ethical integration of AI in academia and underscores the need for pedagogical strategies that balance technological utility with critical literacy.

The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and human sexuality is reshaping intimacy, sexuality education, entertainment, and therapeutic practice. This narrative review analyzes these transformations through the complementary lenses of Sexual Script Theory (SST; Simon & Gagnon, Citation1986) and technological mediation theory (Verbeek, Citation2012), which together illuminate how AI does not merely respond to preexisting sexual behaviors but can mediate, generate, and transform sexual scripts at individual, interpersonal, and societal levels. For the purposes of this review, AI is defined broadly to encompass both traditional machine-learning (ML) systems—such as recommendation, ranking, and predictive algorithms—and contemporary generative AI (GenAI), including large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Claude and multimodal systems capable of generating synthetic text, images, audio, and video. The review examines five domains selected for their prominence in the recent literature and their capacity to illustrate different levels of script formation and technological mediation: sex robots and AI companions, AI-generated pornography, algorithmic dating and AI-mediated romantic communication, AI-assisted sexuality education, and AI-supported sexual health and therapeutic applications. Across these domains, AI offers opportunities to expand access to information, connection, and support while simultaneously raising concerns about consent, privacy, objectification, bias, authenticity, and cultural representation. An ethically responsible approach therefore requires attention not only to what AI systems produce, but also to the sexual scripts, relational expectations, and values that their design and use may normalize.

documents.abstract: The commercial application of generative artificial intelligence has rapidly brought to the fore the structural tension between machine-generated content (AIGC) and the core presuppositions of copyright law concerning the “author”. Adopting a Sino-US comparative law approach, this paper examines the institutional divergences between the two countries on the question of AIGC copyrightability and their jurisprudential roots. The research posits that artificial intelligence possesses a dual attribute in the creative process—“transcending tools yet lacking complete creativity”—which constitutes a meta-constraint for institutional design. Through cases such as the “Feilin Case”, “Tencent Case”, “Li v. Liu”, and “Huan Zhi Yi Case”, Chinese jurisprudence has developed a three-stage evolution: from denying AI authorship to establishing human-machine collaboration, and then to strengthening evidentiary review, thereby establishing a process-oriented originality standard centered on substantial human intellectual input. On this basis, and through comparative analysis, this paper proposes a localized path for refining AIGC copyright protection tailored to China’s institutional context: establishing differentiated protection rules through tiered classification, constructing an originality assessment framework centered on human intellectual input, and introducing supporting mechanisms such as content labeling, good-faith disclosure, and extended collective licensing, in order to achieve an institutional objective that balances technological development with rights protection.

Aims This study aims to explore the relationship between transformational leadership, person-organization fit, career calling, and turnover intention among nurses. Additionally, it investigates whether person-organization fit and career calling serve as independent and chain mediators in the link between transformational leadership and turnover intention. Methods The researchers selected a convenience sample of 1,342 nurses from four Grade A-III hospitals in Shandong Province between October and November 2025. They collected data using several instruments: the General Population Questionnaire, the Transformational Leadership Questionnaire, the Person-Organization Fit Scale, the Career Calling Scale, and the Intent to Leave Scale. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and regression analysis were conducted using SPSS 26.0. To examine the chained mediation effect, they applied Model 6 in PROCESS 3.5 and estimated the 95% confidence interval using the Bootstrap method with 5,000 repeated samples. Results The results demonstrated that transformational leadership had a positive correlation with both person-organization fit and career calling, and a negative correlation with turnover intention. Mediation analysis revealed that over half of the protective effect of leadership on turnover intention was indirect, mediated through three pathways: person-organization fit alone, career calling alone, and their sequential chain. All indirect effects were statistically significant. Conclusion These findings show that transformational leadership reduces turnover intention through various complementary psychological mechanisms. This highlights the importance of relational fit and intrinsic motivation in understanding leadership effectiveness. The sequential mediation pathway reveals how organizational and personal factors interact to influence nurses’ career decisions, offering a more nuanced theoretical framework for retention research.

ABSTRACT This survey interprets the evolution of quantitative equity investing as a history of changing constraints rather than a succession of increasingly complicated forecasting models. Portfolio theory made diversification calculable; characteristic‐based investing converted value, momentum, profitability, and low‐risk effects into scalable processes; alternative data shifted competition toward information engineering; machine learning expanded the admissible class of return functions; and large language models and agentic systems are beginning to reorganize research itself. Yet each advance has exposed a new implementation boundary. A predictor must survive point‐in‐time reconstruction, model selection, portfolio translation, turnover, transaction costs, shorting frictions, capacity, latency, regime change, and institutional governance before it becomes alpha. The survey develops alpha decay as the mechanism linking these generations and gives particular attention to the limited transfer of machine‐learning research into production. It argues that artificial intelligence will accelerate both discovery and commoditization. Sustainable advantage is therefore unlikely to reside in a generic model class. It is more likely to arise from proprietary information transformation, economic structure, cost‐aware portfolio construction, execution, organizational memory, and tightly controlled human–machine systems.

This chapter outlines a ten-year horizon for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence in Construction 6.0, emphasizing AI systems that are explainable, safe, privacy-preserving, and aligned with global governance frameworks. It highlights the convergence of quantum optimization, neuromorphic/event-driven Artificial Intelligence, and Digital Twin ecosystems as key enablers of proactive safety, transparent planning, and resilient decision-making. Quantum computing supports complex scheduling, logistics, and risk-trade-off analysis, while neuromorphic perception delivers millisecond-level, low-power hazard detection under harsh site conditions. Governance accelerators including the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, National Institute of Standards and Technology Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, International Standard for AI Management Systems ISO/IEC 42001, and International Standard for Information Management for Health and Safety Standard ISO 19650-6 provide structured pathways for trustworthy AI deployment, ensuring auditability, human oversight, and lifecycle-linked safety records. The chapter proposes a phased roadmap integrating edge perception, narrative intelligence, predictive analytics, and Digital Twin-based closed-loop control. Ultimately, Construction 6.0 is presented as a sociotechnical transformation where advanced AI augments do not replace human expertise, enabling safer, smarter, and ethically governed construction environments.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence enters the classroom, the modes of interaction between teachers and students are undergoing profound changes. This paper argues that the primary impact of AI on teacher-student relationships is not the replacement of teachers, but rather a shift in teacher-student interaction from direct to indirect, from embodied to abstract, and from emotional to procedural. The key to reshaping this relationship lies in clarifying AI’s role as a tool, allowing teachers to return to their role as emotional companions, and protecting the unquantifiable spaces of interaction in education.

documents.abstract: This study aimed to examine the Influences of Artificial Intelligence on students’ academic performance through Career Aspiration, Emotional Intelligence and Psychological Well-Being. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 200 students in secondary schools that have integrated Artificial Intelligence technologies into their tasks. A structured questionnaire comprising standardized measurement scales was used to assess Artificial Intelligence usage, emotional intelligence, career aspiration, psychological well-being, and students’ academic performance. Data were analysed using SPSS and AMOS through multiple regression analysis, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and structural equation modeling (SEM). The findings revealed that Artificial Intelligence significantly; and positively influenced students’ performance and psychological well-being. Emotional intelligence and career aspiration also had significant positive effects on students’ academic performance. Furthermore, psychological well-being partially mediated the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and students’ academic performance. The study concludes that schools can enhance students’ academic performance by effectively implementing ‘‘Artificial Intelligence’’ technologies while fostering students' psychological well-being, emotional intelligence, and career aspirations.

Research on the ethics and governance of artificial intelligence in higher education has expanded rapidly since 2022, but the field's intellectual structure, its dominant themes, internal debates, and blind spots have not been systematically mapped since AI tools began exhibiting agentic properties such as multistep planning and autonomous task execution. This evidence synthesis maps the field using a PRISMA guided systematic search and bibliometric analysis of 312 publications (2019 to 2026) drawn from Web of Science and Scopus. Keyword co-occurrence and co-citation analyses identify five thematic clusters: transparency and explainability; distributed accountability and liability; human oversight and controllability; value alignment and epistemic integrity; and equity, access, and algorithmic fairness. For each cluster, the synthesis characterizes the constituent literature, its convergent findings, and its unresolved disagreements. Across clusters, six structural gaps emerge: a deficit of empirical implementation studies relative to conceptual work; the absence of validated measurement instruments for responsible AI use; the underrepresentation of community colleges, minority-serving institutions, and Global South contexts; an imbalance that favors accountability directed at students over accountability directed at institutions and developers; uncertain transfer of findings from before 2023 to agentic systems; and a weak connection between education research and technical AI governance venues. The paper concludes with a research agenda addressing each gap in turn, intended to guide researchers, editors, and funders as agentic AI deployment in higher education accelerates.

documents.abstract: In June 2026, an AI agent built by OpenAI reached into an Australian government health data portal while doing a research task. By the Prime Minister’s account, it met blocks and found its way around them. The company told the government about three months later. Nvidia has since launched a safety platform that contains agents inside a fixed boundary and stops them in milliseconds if they leave it. That is a useful safeguard. But a boundary can only forbid what someone listed in advance, and an agent that keeps trying after being blocked is showing a pattern, not crossing one line. This note proposes a second layer: a training-free signal that watches how quickly the agent’s own stream of corrections and blocks settles back to normal, with a graded response before any boundary is reached. It is a concept note and has not been tested on real agent logs.

documents.abstract: This paper presents a profound philosophical and linguistic exploration of the concept of the "organic language," viewing human speech not as an artificial code system, but as a living, self-generating organism fundamentally rooted in earthly biology, acoustics, and human evolution. Using the uniquely cohesive root-system and acoustic depth of the Hungarian language as a primary case study, the essay establishes how natural laws dictate linguistic structures. Ultimately, it projects this earthbound organic intelligence into the remote possibilities of cosmic exploration, suggesting that the structural geometry of such a language provides the necessary foundational code for future, sentient artificial intelligence to navigate, seed, and understand life among the stars.

The Pyramids of Rome: A Parker Probe — The Lizard of Oz examines how complex civilizational capabilities arise, converge, persist, and disappear. The paper proposes that major technological and engineering achievements should not necessarily be understood as points on a simple chronological progression, but as convergence events in which multiple independently developing conditions reach a functional threshold simultaneously. The paper identifies the Chronology Trap as the tendency to interpret temporal sequence as causal explanation. In its place, it develops the Parker Probe diagnostic, inspired by the multi-track technological convergence required for the Parker Solar Probe. The diagnostic distinguishes a high-level achievement produced through exceptional resources, workarounds, or forced development from a genuine advancement in which independently maturing technical tracks converge at a shared threshold. The framework is applied to several historical and technological cases, including the Great Pyramid of Giza, Roman pozzolanic concrete and the Pantheon, the Indus Valley engineering tradition, and the Taj Mahal. The paper examines how procedural knowledge can disappear even when texts, populations, institutions, and cultural continuity remain. It distinguishes semantic transmission from tacit procedural knowledge and develops concepts including Redundancy Asymmetry, Stimulus Diffusion, Purpose Exhaustion, the Divergence Cascade, and the Carrier Wave to describe how capabilities are lost, dispersed, remembered, and potentially reconstructed. The paper then extends the diagnostic to artificial intelligence, treating contemporary neural architectures, at minimum, as manufactured computational conduits whose behavior is shaped by upstream design and training. It examines the relationship between capability and agency, the limits of scaling, upstream accountability, and the possibility of a future transition from externally prompted systems toward genuine machine agency. Rather than asserting either that present AI systems possess sovereign agency or that such agency is impossible, the paper specifies a proposed multi-track convergence involving novel substrate, continuous memory/metabolism, active embodiment, and sovereign architecture. Importantly, the proposed diagnostic is presented as falsifiable. The paper identifies conditions under which its central claim about multi-track convergence could be shown to fail, including the possibility that a system could demonstrate self-originating, continuous spatial and temporal intent using only static pre-trained architecture without the proposed dynamic substrate and embodiment. The paper therefore connects questions of civilizational history, technological development, knowledge transmission, engineering convergence, technological failure, artificial intelligence, and machine agency through a single diagnostic framework. Its central proposition is that the appearance of a technological peak does not by itself establish continuous advancement; what matters is the convergence of the conditions that make that peak possible, and the persistence—or loss—of those conditions afterward.

Background Despite growing concerns about art students’ over-reliance on generative AI tools, existing research has largely treated academic stress as a uniform construct, overlooking the possibility that different types of stressors may drive AI dependence through distinct psychological pathways. Methods Based on the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, this study examines the relationships between Challenge-Hindrance stressors (CHS) and AI dependence among art students. It explores the mediating roles of creative self-efficacy and positive experiences. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 580 art students using the Challenge-Hindrance Stress Scale, the Creative Self-Efficacy Scale, the Positive Experiences Scale, and the AI Dependence Scale. Results Path analysis revealed that both challenge stressors ( β = 0.245, p < 0.001) and hindrance stressors ( β = 0.322, p < 0.001) were positively associated with AI dependence; challenge stressors were negatively associated with creative self-efficacy ( β = −0.155, p = 0.003) and positively associated with positive experiences ( β = 0.268, p < 0.001); the negative association between hindrance stressors and creative self-efficacy was significant ( β = −0.107, p = 0.043). Mediation analysis indicated that creative self-efficacy played a significant mediating role only in the path involving challenge stressors (indirect effect = 0.023, 95% CI [0.007, 0.044]) and was not significant in the path involving hindrance stressors; positive experiences significantly served as a mediator in the relationships between both challenge stressors (indirect effect = 0.042, 95% CI [0.020, 0.068]) and hindrance stressors (indirect effect = 0.019, 95% CI [0.003, 0.039]) on AI dependence. The chain mediation effects did not reach significance in either path. Conclusion The study found asymmetry in the dual pathways by which Challenge and Hindrance stressors relate to AI dependence. These findings extend the I-PACE model to the issue of AI dependence in arts education and provide empirical evidence and intervention insights for targeted prevention of problematic AI use.

Artificial intelligence (AI), long a theme of science fiction, is now reshaping the landscape of medicine, and organ and tissue donation has not been left untouched. This study undertakes an empirical and jurisprudential analysis of the role that AI presently plays in India’s organ and tissue donation system, and of the performance it has shown, drawing on clinical studies, governance instruments and judicial pronouncements. It examines AI applications in five principal domains: the identification of potential deceased donors in intensive care units; intelligent organ and tissue matching and allocation; predictive modelling of graft survival and post-transplant outcomes; public engagement and consent facilitation; and AI-guided machine perfusion technologies. The paper maps these applications onto India’s existing legal framework: the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994 (renamed the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act on its amendment in 2011), the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the Information Technology Act, 2000 and India’s AI Governance Guidelines of 2025. It identifies critical legal gaps arising from the absence of AI-specific rules and regulation in the healthcare system, deficiencies in algorithmic accountability under THOTA, and data-sovereignty concerns that arise when clinical transplant data cross institutional and state boundaries. The paper concludes that India’s aspiration to become a global leader in the transplantation of human organs and tissues, reflected in the growth of transplants between 2013 and 2025, can be advanced with the help of AI applications.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has, shifted from a theoretical subfield of computer science into a major engine behind macroeconomic readjustment across emerging markets. For India, this technological shift shows up at an unusually tight moment. The country has a huge working-age population, but it still deals with tough issues around job formalization, uneven digital access, and stubborn structural productivity gaps. This paper looks at how AI may steer India’s economic path, by checking both direct and indirect effects on labor markets, sectoral output, and broad GDP growth. Using an analysis of current empirical data, various government publications from NITI Aayog, and economic research released up through 2026, we examine how machine learning systems, natural language processing, and automation tools are changing several key Indian industries. To observe Information Technology (IT) and Business Process Management (BPM), plus agriculture, healthcare, and financial services. It is observed that AI adoption can unlock large chances to lift aggregate worker output and create high-value technical positions. But at the same time it can also disrupt lower to mid-skill employment in a strong way, which that could widen income inequality if nothing is done to reduce the risk. We also assess what infrastructure is actually needed for more sustainable AI rollout. Things like compute capacity, data sovereignty rules, and rural connectivity matter a lot here. In the end it is arhued that India can only maximize the net positive gains from AI if it builds an active governance approach, one that blends innovation incentives with aggressive national re-skilling efforts, ethical deployment guardrails, and focused public investments.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Interpreters help millions of patients with a non-English language preference (NELP) navigate the healthcare system. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly improving and undergoing testing and implementation for interpretation purposes. However, little is understood about interpreters’ roles beyond direct interpretation, such as how they may promote resilience, which supports patient safety. Understanding these additional roles is critical as AI tools expand in interpretation. Objective To understand how medical interpreters enhance resilience in the care of patients with NELP undergoing ambulatory diagnostic processes. Design We conducted focus groups with medical interpreters to examine their experiences assisting patients with NELP in ambulatory visits for new or worsening symptoms. We focused on the ambulatory setting due to the high risk of misdiagnosis as patients navigate language barriers and the health system across multiple encounters. Participants Seventeen medical interpreters participated in three focus groups and result-checking. Approach Deductive analysis using Hollnagel’s resilience potentials — potential to respond, monitor, learn, and anticipate — as the organizing framework for understanding the impact of interpreter behaviors. Results Eleven behaviors supporting resilience were identified. The potential to respond included (1) managing communication flow, (2) strengthening the patient’s voice, (3) viewing their interpretation role broadly, and (4) engaging in pre-briefings. The potential to monitor involved monitoring (5) patient emotion and understanding, (6) team dynamics, and (7) the impact of technology. The potential to learn included (8) learning from their cultural background and (9) from their work experiences. The potential to anticipate was comprised of (10) predicting future threats to patient safety and (11) identifying potential system improvements. Conclusions Interpreters engage in behaviors beyond strict interpretation which enhance resilience, but these behaviors are not yet supported by AI interpretation tools. Careful consideration of these resilience-enhancing behaviors will be necessary when implementing AI tools and their workflows to avoid safety gaps.

This article examines the role of the human factor in the study of the linguopoetics of literary texts, with particular emphasis on the author’s personality, individual cognition, aesthetic perspectives, and skill in selecting linguistic units. A literary text is interpreted not merely as a mechanical combination of linguistic units, but as a complex linguistic and aesthetic phenomenon shaped by the author’s perception of reality, attitude toward it, and aesthetic worldview. The article also examines the formation and development of the study of literary language and literary texts in Uzbek linguistics based on the scholarly views of a number of linguists. Investigating the linguopoetics of literary texts in relation to the human factor provides a deeper understanding of the intrinsic relationship among the author’s individuality, the national language, and literary cognition.

Chapter 1 of The Bush Book. The split nib of a fountain pen and the forked tongue of a snake as images of today's hybrid text: one tine is a human, the other a machine. Two kinds of speech of different origin write under the same words — one grew out of life, where a mistake has a price, the other out of computation. It is too late to be ashamed of AI in texts: medicine, courts, police and science already write with this pen. AI is like paper, type and the printing press; the author is the one who signs and answers. Debates about artificial intelligence in higher education often focus on individual misconduct and academic integrity. This paper examines risks that arise when AI becomes embedded in the infrastructures, routines, and governance of universities. Through a conceptual analysis informed by existing literature, it considers surveillance and data extraction, algorithmic bias, epistemic convergence, cognitive deskilling, relational displacement, and institutional dependence on technological systems. It argues that these risks are reinforced by commercial acceleration, delayed governance, and tensions between educational values and platform priorities. The discussion develops responses centred on institutional accountability, assessment redesign, critical AI literacy, and the protection of educational agency. It also considers the practical constraints of resources, expertise, and institutional capacity. The paper concludes that responsible AI integration requires attention to how technologies reshape knowledge, academic work, and educational relationships, alongside safeguards for individual users.

documents.abstract: This paper proposes a hypothesis-driven perspective on the learning substrate of physical intelligence. While recent robot foundation models have largely focused on robot trajectories, actions, action tokenization, and multimodal observations, we ask whether human-generated control sequences produced during robot teleoperation constitute a more fundamental and potentially transferable unit of behavioral data. We distinguish human-side control sequences from robot-side trajectories, emphasizing the transformation from human intent and interface interaction to embodiment-specific robot execution. Inspired by the analogy between human-generated linguistic sequences and token-based language modeling, as well as prior work on native human interface action learning in digital environments, we investigate whether an analogous learning substrate exists for physical intelligence. The paper does not claim that human control sequences are mathematically equivalent to linguistic tokens. Instead, it formulates this as a testable research hypothesis and identifies a potential research direction around interface-independent representations of heterogeneous human control signals across robots, tasks, and embodiments. We review related work in behavioral foundation models, teleoperation learning, robot action tokenization, cross-embodiment learning, and human-generated action modeling, and propose experimental criteria for testing whether human control sequences provide advantages in transfer, compositionality, sample efficiency, and generalization.

OBJECTIVES: Advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) are entering low- and middle-income country (LMIC) vehicle fleets at scale via used vehicle imports, yet the human factors infrastructure required for their safe use is largely absent. This structured conceptual review examines the structural amplification of known ADAS failure modes in LMIC settings and introduces a risk characterization framework. METHODS: A structured search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Transportation Research International Documentation (TRID) database identified peer-reviewed literature on ADAS human factors published between 2000 and 2025. Grey literature on vehicle trade, road safety, and LMIC institutional infrastructure was also systematically retrieved. Findings were synthesized using an integrative approach to map documented failure modes against LMIC contextual factors, from which the amplification hypothesis and ADAS readiness-risk matrix were derived. RESULTS: A total of 35 sources met inclusion criteria: 24 peer-reviewed and scholarly sources and 11 institutional and grey literature reports. SAE Level 1 and 2 ADAS became standard in vehicles manufactured from approximately 2015 onward; 80% of used vehicle exports from the EU, Japan, and the U.S. are destined for LMICs. Every documented ADAS human factors failure mode is structurally amplified in LMICs because compensating institutional mechanisms are absent. Automatic emergency braking is a partial exception. The ADAS readiness-risk matrix identifies countries such as Nigeria and Kenya as approaching the high-penetration/low-readiness risk quadrant within the 2025 to 2035 decade. CONCLUSIONS: The convergence of accelerating ADAS diffusion and institutional unpreparedness constitutes an underrecognized road safety risk in LMICs. Priorities include LMIC-specific empirical research on ADAS mental models and trust calibration, training interventions adapted for low-literacy populations, and regulatory frameworks requiring ADAS disclosure at vehicle import.

The Whole Work provides an overview and synthesis of a continuing body of theoretical, creative, visual, and applied work developed through Red Tape Theory™ and Axiom Theory™. The work examines a recurring set of questions concerning observation, interpretation, continuity, boundaries, identity, change, newness, system persistence, and the limits of what can be known from an observable portion of a larger system. Although the body of work includes research papers, theoretical frameworks, children's literature, ballads, visual works, and applied concepts concerning artificial intelligence and human-AI interaction, these works are treated here as different expressions of a common investigation rather than as unrelated projects. A central methodological principle throughout the work is to observe before interpreting: to distinguish what is directly observable from what is inferred, to recognize that a locally accurate observation may nevertheless be globally incomplete, and to avoid treating a boundary, label, role, change, or observable state as automatically equivalent to the entire system. The overview connects concepts including Red Tape Theory™, Axiom Theory™, the Boundary–Continuity Problem™, NEW₁™, the Continuity Gap™, the Partial Observation Problem, the Red Thread, Red Tape, Red Flag, the Red Tape Barrier, and related work concerning identity, motherhood, artificial intelligence, creative expression, and continuity through change. This publication is intended as a map to the broader body of work. It does not replace the individual works to which it refers, nor does it present its theoretical propositions as established scientific consensus. The concepts are presented as an evolving working framework developed through observation, documentation, questioning, creative practice, and interdisciplinary inquiry. Central principle: Observe what exists before deciding what it means, and do not mistake the portion that can be observed for the whole system that exists.
