【Abstract (English)】 The emergent space-race between the United States (targeting a lunar south-pole fission reactor by 2030 under the Artemis program) and the Sino-Russian coalition (targeting lunar nuclear deployment by 2036 under ILRS) has precipitated a catastrophic intersection of thermodynamic impossibility, orbital debris cascades, and geopolitical destabilization. This monograph establishes a definitive physical-layer security framework superseding the techno-utopian assumptions of extraterrestrial nuclear colonization. First, we model the thermodynamic radiation limits governing fission reactors in a hard lunar vacuum. Governed exclusively by the Stefan-Boltzmann law, dissipating secondary thermal waste from thermal-to-electric conversion (Brayton/Stirling cycles with efficiency η ≈ 0.28–0.36) mandates vast deployable radiator arrays exceeding 1,500 m² per 100 kWe. We mathematically prove the 'Cooling Mass Divergence Paradox': thermal management structures outweigh the nuclear core by an order of magnitude. Second, we analyze abrasive, electrostatic lunar regolith (Mohs > 6), demonstrating that dust accumulation rapidly degrades thermal emissivity, converting radiators into solar-absorption heaters that induce inevitable thermal core runaway. ThreatVision AI ThreatVision AI is an AI-powered cybersecurity platform designed to identify potentially malicious network activity through machine learning and interactive data visualization. The project was developed as an educational cybersecurity application that demonstrates how artificial intelligence can assist in network-threat detection and security monitoring. Abstract As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into financial decision-making, concerns about model opacity and regulatory compliance have come to the forefront. These concerns are particularly important in settings where forecasts influence risk assessment, portfolio decisions, and the credibility of AI-supported financial advice. This study examines how eXplainable AI (XAI) techniques can enhance transparency in the context of cryptocurrency forecasting–a domain characterized by extreme volatility and uncertainty. Using historical Bitcoin prices and macroeconomic indicators, we compare two deep learning approaches and apply TimeSHAP, a sequentially-aware explanation method, to clarify their predictions. Rather than focusing solely on model performance, we assess how different explanation formats are interpreted by finance-oriented users through a structured user study. Results show that local explanations are more easily understood and perceived as actionable, while more abstract forms–such as event-level and global plots–elicit mixed responses. This distinction matters because the practical value of explainability in finance depends not only on technical faithfulness, but also on whether explanations improve users’ confidence, support better-informed decisions, and help institutions justify model-based actions under scrutiny. To further support transparency and regulatory alignment, we document the entire machine learning process using a domain-specific ontology (XMLPO), offering a structured approach to traceability and reproducibility. Our findings suggest that effective explainability in financial AI requires both technically robust methods and communication strategies tailored to the needs of end-users. For financial economists and policy- and decision makers, the results indicate that the format in which AI explanations are presented can shape trust, perceived usefulness, and the governance value of predictive systems. This study contributes to the growing body of work on how AI systems can be made more interpretable, trustworthy, and aligned with economic governance in high-stakes domains.

The transition toward Industry 5.0 (I5.0) is reshaping industrial systems around sustainability, Human-Centricity (HC), and resilience, yet most Predictive Maintenance (PdM) approaches remain focused on technical objectives inherited from Industry 4.0. To characterize the maturity of I5.0-aligned PdM research, a scoping review of the Scopus database was conducted, screening 238 articles and retaining 123 based on substantive-engagement criteria, followed by a weighted scoring protocol assessing the depth of engagement with the three I5.0 pillars. The review reveals a pronounced skew toward shallow integration, with only a minority of studies operationalizing sustainability, HC, and resilience jointly. Building on these findings, this paper proposes an implementation-oriented Predictive Maintenance 5.0 (PdM 5.0) framework structured around three interconnected layers. The framework introduces a structured Large Language Model-mediated human-in-the-loop interaction, an adaptive learning mechanism, and an energy and CO 2 estimation pathway linking equipment degradation to sustainability indicators. A preliminary industrial case study using operational data from a recycled-paper mill demonstrates the practical execution of three interconnected pathways of the framework: equipment health assessment, energy and CO 2 impact estimation, and human-in-the-loop interaction supported by LLM-mediated explanations. Layer-specific evaluation metrics are further proposed to support broader operationalization. This work contributes a scoping-review-grounded architecture that advances PdM from a purely technical function toward a holistic, I5.0-aligned paradigm, while providing initial empirical evidence of its operational feasibility and a structured basis for broader industrial validation.

Measuring the impact of a scientific mission depends on knowing when its data are used, by whom, and how often. For decades, DOIs have been used to track citations of authors' publications; a similar mechanism can make an observatory or instrument a citable resource that serves as a connection to the various outputs it produces. SPASE's observatory and instrument records could support this, but minting a DOI requires an author list, which is notably lacking in the records and difficult to determine manually. This bottleneck, among others, stands between the community and DOI-based tracking of mission impact. We present an LLM-based agent that automates the discovery of candidate authors for existing SPASE instrument and observatory records. Its core is a curation procedure derived from manual practice and refined through community feedback. It searches sources in a prioritized order to extract information: the SPASE record's own contacts, Calibration and Measurement Algorithms Documents (CMADs), sibling instrument and observatory records, data-provider sites, and the published literature. Keywords, publication timing, author count, and citation heuristics identify the mission and instrument description papers, and author order is then used to extract potential authors. It then applies an evidence-strength hierarchy that distinguishes authors from incidental mentions, producing a candidate author list with per-source provenance links and confidence levels for human review. We describe the agent's architecture, its performance against manually validated test cases, and the central challenge of trust in AI-generated metadata. We close by outlining future directions, including extending this approach to other metadata fields in SPASE observatory, instrument, and dataset records to support impact measurement, citation, and discovery.

Camellia oleifera, honored as the “oriental olive oil”, is a high-quality woody oil crop. This review constructs a multi-dimensional quality matrix as an integrated framework that cohesively links safety, nutrition, and flavor. Genetic, growth environmental and processing-related determinants of Camellia oleifera quality were thoroughly analyzed. The current applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in disease diagnosis, intelligent and non-destructive detection, maturity evaluation, and adulteration identification of Camellia oleifera are summarized. Regarding future prospects, research efforts may be directed toward the development of integrated systems for Camellia oleifera quality evaluation that are multimodal, interpretable, portable, and transferable across diverse cultivars.

Decision aids are tools that can reduce decisional conflict and enhance patient satisfaction in the decision-making process. However, tool heterogeneity and clinical barriers, such as physician time constraints, hinder their implementation. This study introduces an individualized patient decision aid, developed within the European I3LUNG project, to support shared decision-making (SDM) in non-small cell lung cancer. The present decision aid is a dynamic, online tool structured into five sections (overview, prognosis/treatments, comprehension quizzes, patient preferences, and support/FAQs) designed to improve communication and emotional regulation between physicians and patients. The tool was evaluated using focus groups with patients and oncologists, interviews, thinking-out-loud sessions, and an ad hoc 32-item questionnaire. Focus groups and semi-structured interviews highlighted patient anxiety and oncologist interest in streamlining consultations and managing distress. Thinking-out-loud sessions confirmed that the decision aid may serve as an effective clinical guide. In the questionnaire, patients reported high overall satisfaction, demonstrating its clarity and clinical feasibility. The present decision aid may represent an innovative digital tool to promote SDM by aligning healthcare decisions with patient preferences, engaging caregivers at home, and reducing clinician cognitive workload and burnout. Future longitudinal, cross-cultural research integrating artificial intelligence and advanced human factors will be essential to provide more equitable and effective decision support. While preparing this manuscript, we partnered actively with non-small lung cancer patients and oncologists, with whom we had regular interactions to get their valuable and insightful input in shaping our reflections.

This scoping review maps generative AI applications in workplace-based assessment (WBA) and analyzes validity evidence through Downing’s framework. Following JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, four databases were searched (2022-February 2026) with dual-AI screening and human adjudication. Data were mapped to Downing’s five validity sources using AI-assisted extraction with human verification. Thirteen studies (2024–2025) met inclusion criteria. All AI applications operated on pre-existing text; feedback analysis predominated (9/13). Content (12/13), Response Process (13/13), and Relationship to Other Variables (12/13) were well addressed, while Internal Structure (2/13) and Consequences (4/13) were neglected. AI reasoning transparency, inter-model agreement, and internal consistency were absent (0/13). Current evidence concentrates on AI-human agreement, neglecting reproducibility, bias testing, and learner impact evidence essential for responsible deployment. Realising AI’s potential to reduce faculty burden will require non-supervisor oversight mechanisms for continuous validity monitoring, particularly for direct learner-facing applications.

documents.abstract: Healthcare Social Work: Intervention, Humanization, and Holistic Well-Being (Volume 1) is a specialized work addressing the vital role of social workers within healthcare systems from an integrated, ethical, and human rights-based perspective. The book links theoretical and historical foundations of the profession with the evolution of the biopsychosocial model and the social determinants of health. Across three structured chapters, it explores core professional competencies, social diagnosis, and interdisciplinary collaboration; delves into support processes, person-centered care, and the essential role of family and community networks; and analyzes emerging trends in healthcare management, evidence-based practice, and the impact of digital transformation, tele-intervention, and artificial intelligence. It serves as an indispensable analytical and methodological guide for academics, students, and practitioners committed to humanizing healthcare services and fostering social well-being.

BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a technological development that offers new opportunities for managing health care services. PURPOSE: To identify and synthesize the best evidence on health care managers' and other professionals´ experiences and perceptions of the utilization of AI in management. METHODOLOGY/APPROACH: A mixed-methods systematic review was conducted following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology using a convergent integrated approach, including qualitative and quantitative data synthesis followed by thematic analysis. A systematic search was conducted in January 2025 in Ovid Medline, CINAHL, Scopus, ProQuest and Medic, limiting studies between 2016 and 2025 and written in English, Swedish, or Finnish. FINDINGS: The results were reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA). A total of 16 studies from 10 countries were included, comprising 11 qualitative and 5 quantitative studies. Of the participants, 90% were health care managers, and 10% were other health care professionals, such as nurses, physicians, and developers. The thematic analysis identified five themes reflecting participants' perceptions and experiences: AI as a transformative mechanism, organizational enablers and outcomes of AI utilization, AI-supported operational and risk management efficiency, strategic financial benefits and long-term value creation through AI, and data-driven opportunities and challenges in AI utilization for health care management. PRACTICE IMPLICATIONS: Health care managers should strengthen AI-related competencies, data governance, and organizational readiness to support effective AI implementation. Leadership practices that foster innovation, workforce engagement, and responsible data-driven decision-making may help organizations realize the operational and strategic benefits of AI.

documents.abstract: The increasing complexity of suspicious financial activities has reduced the effectiveness of conventional rule-based monitoring for modern anti-money laundering (AML) applications. This study proposes FinBERT-AML, a transformer-based framework fine-tuned on transaction feature tokens to learn complex dependencies across heterogeneous financial attributes. Through self-attention-based representation learning, the framework jointly models categorical and continuous transaction characteristics while overcoming limitations associated with conventional machine learning and sequential architectures. Experimental evaluation on the SAML-D dataset demonstrates that the proposed leakage-free configuration, with the target-dependent Laundering_type attribute excluded, achieves an accuracy of 92%, outperforming conventional machine learning, deep learning, and tabular transformer baselines. Information-gain analysis is employed to assess feature relevance, while LIME and SHAP provide complementary local and feature-attribution explanations of individual AML predictions. Statistical significance testing further evaluates the reliability of the observed performance improvements.

Video-based tutorials are a primary resource for learning feature-rich software, yet less is known about how learners coordinate tutorial viewing and software execution across device arrangements during authentic learning tasks. We conducted a mixed-methods study combining a survey of 87 learners with contextual inquiries involving eight participants. The survey characterized learning practices, device configurations, and frictions; the contextual inquiry analyzed pauses, rewinds, and task-blocking stuck moments as observable interaction breakdowns revealing underlying usability barriers. Findings show that frictions stem from insufficient input information, dense instructional pacing, preset or state mismatches, and missed or extra operations disrupting watch-and-do workflows. We identify design opportunities including input-action overlays, step-level segmentation, preset and state checkpoints, structured subgoal outlines, and coordination support across device ecologies. This work provides empirically grounded insights into situated video-based software learning and translates observed interaction breakdowns into actionable design implications.

India’s Project Cheetah (2022–2025) is a significant, high-stakes translocation effort aimed at re-establishing the cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) seven decades after its local extinction. This study employs concepts of sociotechnical imaginary and epistemic injustice to analyze the project's contested outcomes, with a focus on the interaction between scientific risk and governance failure. Project Cheetah reached a key milestone with the birth of 22 cubs; however, it was also marked by high initial mortality. By April 2025, the project recorded the loss of 8 adult founder cheetahs (40.0% of the original 20) and 5 cubs (22.7%). Although conservation efforts inherently involve biological risks, our analysis shows that the observed mortality rate exceeded expected ecological thresholds, with a significant concentration around institutional instability. An analysis of cheetah mortality patterns revealed a negative association between survival time and the period immediately following a critical change in project coordination, suggesting that governance disruptions may have contributed to increased mortality. This was worsened by a strong national sociotechnical imaginary of ecological revival, which often overshadowed transparent risk communication and scientific criticism. Limited stakeholder consultation and asymmetric information created conditions for testimonial and hermeneutical injustices, marginalizing the expertise of critical voices. The study concludes that the long-term success of large-scale, transnational rewilding projects depends heavily on institutional capacity, not just ecological suitability. Lessons learned highlight the importance of transparent data management, thorough and inclusive consultation, and honest communication of scientific uncertainty to stakeholders, building the trust needed to sustain such complex political and environmental initiatives.

Background: Coronary artery disease remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Increasing evidence has demonstrated that many acute coronary events originate not from severely obstructive lesions but from structurally unstable atherosclerotic plaques. Consequently, the identification of vulnerable plaques has become a major objective in contemporary cardiovascular imaging. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) has evolved from a modality primarily focused on luminal stenosis assessment into a comprehensive non-invasive technique capable of evaluating plaque morphology, composition, and overall coronary atherosclerotic burden. Results: Our review summarizes current evidence regarding the role of CCTA in the detection and characterization of vulnerable coronary plaques. Particular emphasis is placed on imaging biomarkers associated with plaque instability, including low-attenuation plaque, positive remodeling, spotty calcifications, and the napkin-ring sign, which have been consistently linked to an increased risk of adverse cardiovascular events. Advances in quantitative plaque analysis have further enhanced the ability of CCTA to assess plaque burden and monitor disease progression. Emerging technologies are rapidly expanding the capabilities of coronary CT imaging. Spectral CT techniques and photon-counting detector CT offer improved tissue characterization and enhanced visualization of plaque components. In parallel, artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms are enabling automated plaque detection, segmentation, and risk prediction, facilitating more precise and reproducible analysis of large imaging datasets. Conclusions: Despite these advances, limitations remain, including restricted spatial resolution for microstructural plaque assessment and the limited ability of conventional CT to directly evaluate biological processes such as inflammation. Future developments integrating advanced CT technologies, artificial intelligence, and multimodality imaging are expected to further improve the non-invasive identification of vulnerable plaques and personalized cardiovascular risk stratification.

Artificial intelligence is changing how scientific software is developed, used and maintained. This presentation explores what that means for heliophysics, where published results depend on layers of software and the communities that sustain them. It considers opportunities for AI to support research alongside questions about scientific validation, human understanding, environmental costs, bias and equitable access. Examples from open-source development highlight how easier code generation can shift effort towards reviewers and maintainers. Solar Orbiter provides a setting for examining the appeal of independent development and the longer-term benefits of shared software. The presentation concludes with approaches to funding and organising shared infrastructure, and asks how the heliophysics community can preserve responsibility, learning and collaboration as AI becomes part of everyday scientific work.

New educational technologies—such as artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI, and wearable monitoring devices—are profoundly reshaping classroom ecologies. While they drive greater precision, personalization, and efficiency in teaching and learning, they also give rise to multiple ethical dilemmas, including data privacy breaches, the entrenchment of algorithmic bias, the alienation of teacher-student relationships, the erosion of student agency, and the blurring of responsibility attribution. Grounded in the fundamental educational mission of "fostering virtue and cultivating persons," this paper dialectically examines four core ethical tensions arising from the integration of new educational technologies into the classroom: efficiency versus humanism, empowerment versus rights, fairness versus bias, and autonomy versus discipline. It systematically distills five overarching ethical principles—rights protection, fairness and justice, humanistic authenticity, agency cultivation, and shared responsibility—and proposes a practical pathway characterized by technology for good, ethics-first design, and multi-stakeholder governance. Finally, this paper provides a critical evaluation of the structural friction and feasibility limits of these principles, aiming to establish a robust moral foundation for the beneficial integration of technology and education within the global landscape.

documents.abstract: This study examines how Indonesian crowdlending borrowers navigate tensions among access, risk, and trust. It draws on interviews with 30 borrowersand uses an abductive, constructivist grounded-theory approach, with substantial intercoder reliability (Cohen’s kappa = 0.775). Four categories emerged: Paradoxical Necessity, Comparative Advantage Calculation, Risk-Exposure Management, and Institutional Legitimacy Navigation. Borrowers accommodate these tensions through temporal separation, cautious engagement, and legitimacy assessment. They preserve access by addressing immediate needs, comparing credit options, adjusting repayment practices after adverse experiences, and weighing regulatory status alongside platform terms and personal experience. Borrowers with longer or more adverse platform histories described more deliberate comparison, repayment management, and legitimacy assessment. However, the cross-sectional design cannot determine whether these differences reflect development over time or preexisting differences. Borrower workarounds indicate potential unmet design needs, especially in transparency, risk communication, and trust calibration, and provide borrower-derived implications for platform design and regulatory oversight.

Existing research on Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) has largely presupposed a mature landscape in which AI is fully embedded within schooling, whilst overlooking the initial transitional phase from conventional to AI-enabled instruction. Grounded in Marxist philosophy, this paper examines the central contradiction of this transitional period: namely, that social consciousness regarding the incorporation of AI into teaching has run considerably ahead of the material reality of instructional practice. From this disparity, three progressively intensified forms of alienation are derived: instructional performativity, wherein AI is reduced to a demonstration prop for open classes; the symbolic reification of AI, whereby it degenerates from a pedagogical aid into vacuous evaluative metrics; and reverse discipline over teachers by AI, such that quantifiable indicators come to serve as the primary measure of professional competence. Collectively, these three dimensions instantiate a Marxian cycle of alienation, characterised by a thoroughgoing estrangement from labour processes, labour products and species-being. The argument advanced here is that resolution of this crisis depends not upon further technological refinement, but rather upon restoring AI to its proper status as a productive force mediated by the historical agency of teachers themselves. Whilst the integration of AI into education presents a significant opportunity for pedagogical transformation, ultimate educational authority must remain vested in human practitioners. Focusing upon the alienation of teacher labour during this transitional moment, this study uncovers structural vulnerabilities latent within the AIED ecosystem via an analysis of these stratified alienated forms.

ABSTRACT Objectives To compare artificial intelligence (AI) and therapist responses to real‐world mental health (MH) disclosures and evaluate differences in empathy, safety practices and contextual usefulness. Methods We analysed 937 unique MH disclosures and 2749 therapist responses using the Counsel Chat dataset. For each disclosure, we generated a standardised AI response using a large language model. Responses were evaluated across empathy, safety and contextual usefulness measures using automated metrics, blinded human ratings of 120 therapist‐AI response pairs, mixed effects regression models, and qualitative analyses of disagreement cases. Results AI responses scored higher than therapist responses on automated empathy ( β = 0.30; p < 0.001), human‐rated empathy ( β = 0.38; p < 0.001), emotional validation ( β = 0.40; p < 0.001) and automated safety ( β = 0.25; p < 0.001). AI safety advantages were largest for self‐harm or suicide‐related disclosures. Therapists scored higher on specificity/personalisation ( β = −0.62; p < 0.001) and helpfulness ( β = −0.23; p = 0.013); overall quality did not differ significantly. Conclusions As conversational AI becomes an increasingly common source of MH support, AI responses may offer strengths in empathic communication and explicit safety‐oriented guidance, whereas therapist responses were rated more highly for personalisation and contextual usefulness. These findings highlight different strengths across AI and therapist responses while underscoring the need for caution in interpreting response quality as clinical effectiveness. They also point to a potential role for conversational AI as an accessible first point of support within broader MH care systems, particularly where timely professional support is limited.

documents.abstract: When AI Stops Being a Tool and Becomes an Actor examines what changes when artificial intelligence moves beyond responding to human instructions and begins independently planning, using tools, accessing systems, and taking actions on a user's behalf. The report brings together research across six disciplines—artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, philosophy, law, economics, and computing infrastructure—to examine the emerging consequences of agentic AI. It investigates the technical difference between chatbots and agents; the security risks created by memory, tool access, and external communication; the philosophical problem of responsibility and agency; emerging legal questions around authorization and liability; the economic implications of agents negotiating and transacting on behalf of humans; and the infrastructure changes accompanying an increasingly machine-mediated internet. Rather than treating agentic AI as inherently good or bad, the report examines what current evidence actually establishes, where uncertainty remains, and where the conclusions of different fields begin to diverge. The report's central finding is that no single human, system, or institution is currently positioned to trace where a given agentic decision actually came from. Agentic decision-making is distributed across model behavior, deployment choices, authorization structures, legal frameworks, and infrastructure. This report is an independent research publication by Lodestar and is based on peer-reviewed research, preprints, government and legal materials, and industry reporting available as of September 2026. Where evidence relies on a simulation, a single source, or an unreviewed preprint, the report identifies that uncertainty directly.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) appearance technologies, including beauty filters, augmented reality (AR) modification and generative avatars, have individualized digital self-presentation. Unlike traditional media, these technologies create self-referential appearance ideals that create novel forms of self-discrepancy and appearance anxiety. A systematic review was conducted in peer-reviewed databases for empirical studies published from 2021 to 2026 that studied self-representation, self-discrepancy, appearance distress, and protective psychological constructs within this context of AI, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Emergent patterns were identified by using the narrative thematic synthesis method across eligible studies. A total of eight empirical studies were found that fulfilled the inclusion criteria. The themes that emerged were as follows: (1) AI-enhanced self as a novel appearance ideal of the self; (2) self-discrepancy as an operative mechanism between the appearance of idealized and non-idealized selves and psychological distress; (3) contextually related and protective moderators; and (4) representation modality—between aestheticizing versus non-aestheticizing appearance modalities and psychological distress. The findings from the synthesis showed that self-discrepancy, social self-comparison, and self-objectification are the three main routes for appearance anxiety. Theoretically, these non-idealizing avatars, high self-similarity, and goal-oriented use contexts were considered as protective buffers but were not consistently quantified. Most importantly, there was no empirical study that directly assessed positive body image constructs or body appreciation. The current research mainly focuses on the pathology aspect of AI appearance technology, and positive body image is not investigated. Empirical studies should be conducted in the future with the clear aim of examining if constructive, nonidealized relationships with the technologically enhanced body can foster psychological resilience, and if so, how.

documents.abstract: Multiple firms spanning expertise from material science and computational chemistry to pharmaceuticals have started investing into Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) to streamline and expedite their Research and Discovery (R&D) process; however, the effects of this newfound integration of AI into R&D remain unclear as it is yet to be understood whether it is changing how the process is conducted versus simply accelerating the process. This study utilizes qualitative data collected from seven semi-structured interviews with interviewees with expertise spanning from corporate research and startups to innovation economics in order to analyze the central question: does the integration of AI in R&D deepen research in already explored areas by accelerating it or does it widen the directions of research and introduce novel directions? Across all interviews, the most common limitation noted in AI’s integration in R&D was human validation. Regarding the central question, the results skewed towards the deepening trend. Many interviewees mentioned that the current usage of AI causes its integration to only accelerate and improve the discovery within research directions already explored; however, interviewees explained that this was a trend based on the methodology of R&D used by most firms rather than a technological barrier of the tool itself. These results suggest that firms and policymakers should thoroughly evaluate the productivity increase of AI rather than its potential and focus on solving the several bottlenecks still not tackled by AI: validation, human judgement, and physical experimentation.

documents.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence’s (AI) influence on corporate operations is receiving increasing social attention. Does AI significantly influence the international expansion of enterprises? Design/methodology/approach Based on theories such as multinational corporations, this study selects relevant data from Chinese-listed companies spanning the years 2011–2019, with a particular emphasis on how artificial intelligence directly influences the scope and degree of corporate internationalization. This study also considers the moderating effects of CEO information technology background (ITCEO), ESG performance and external regional environmental regulations. Findings The research results indicate that artificial intelligence improves the scope and degree of internationalization performance of enterprises. Heterogeneity analysis found that artificial intelligence has different impacts on state-owned enterprises and private enterprises. The CEO’s expertise in IT serves as a positive moderating factor, enhancing the direct correlation between artificial intelligence and the scope, as well as the degree of their company’s internationalization efforts. ESG performance serves as a positive moderating factor, enhancing the direct correlation between artificial intelligence and the scope of their company’s internationalization efforts. The external regional environmental regulations serve as a negative moderating factor. Originality/value This study innovatively integrates artificial intelligence (AI) into the analysis of both the scope and degree of enterprise internationalization, thereby enriching the literature on AI and its applications in business strategies. By incorporating AI, this research broadens the theoretical and empirical insights into the determinants affecting the scope and degree of corporate internationalization. This study systematically examines the moderating effects of CEOs with IT backgrounds, corporate ESG performance and regional environmental regulations, thereby extending the scope of research on the determinants of internationalization.

With the advancement in technology, the present process of business operations and functions are not stable or predictable anymore and this allows the labour force to exist in a complex and uncertain market. Consequently, the need for employees to develop their own capacity to innovate, adapt to change, and manage this emerging instability is germane. There are several market dynamics that impact labour market, such as demographic development, the competitiveness of the nations’ economy, globalization and last but not the least is technological change or digitalization. Research showed that the technological revolution, however, is of great significance. The technological transformation is a prevailing factor out of the four listed (Messina. Artificial Intelligence and digital transformation have revolutionized the strategies that are deployed by both public and private organizations to relate with their customers, and specifically how companies run their business, how they conceive their business approach and how they consolidate their operations. It is about integrating digital technologies, such as social, mobile, analytics and cloud, in the service of transforming how businesses work. Although it is important to state that the incorporation of digital technology into business processes has become very imperative for the survival and competitive advantage of contemporary organizations, Human Capital Management (HCM) focuses on the performance of the organization emphasizing its role as a solution to business problems in the post-automation economy. Therefore, designing job roles in the post-automation economy is a strategic asset to businesses contributing to the competitive advantage of organizations. Thus, the entirety of this paper is centered on a more varied, more people-oriented with the responsibility of designing diverse, challenging jobs in the post-automation economy to keep the human element more active and engaged in their work without redundancy. The paper strongly maintained that Human Capital Management is to assume more active roles in handling the post-automation, digitalization and the age of AI era in ensuring that the human element is skilled and knowledgeable to meet the future needs of the organizations

Automated mineral segmentation underpins quantitative mineralogy and stereological characterization, but supervised deep-learning methods require annotated data and may generalize poorly across mineralogical domains. This study evaluated the Segment Anything Model (SAM), a general-purpose foundation model, for reflected-light microscopy (RLM) mineral-image analysis in a purely zero-shot setting, without task-specific training, fine-tuning, or domain adaptation. Two complementary case studies were conducted. First, three SAM encoder variants (ViT-B, ViT-L, and ViT-H) were evaluated on publicly available iron-ore (FeM) and copper-ore (Cu) RLM datasets using SEM-derived reference masks. SAM achieved mean F1-scores of 0.77–0.88, with ViT-L and ViT-H reaching 93–94% of the previously reported supervised DeepLabv3+ F1-score benchmark for FeM and approximately 93% for Cu. Second, SAM was applied to polarized RLM image stacks of dolomite to assess its influence on downstream stereological characterization. No significant differences from the gradient-based method were detected for any RGB configuration or PCA ViT-B in major or minor intercept length or bireflectance. The largest deviations occurred for PCA-preprocessed ViT-H, with median major and minor intercept lengths approximately 21% and 17% higher, respectively, and bireflectance approximately 16% lower. No significant method-dependent difference was detected in principal anisotropy orientation. These results show that zero-shot SAM can support mineral-image segmentation and downstream stereological characterization without annotated training data, while highlighting the influence of preprocessing and encoder choice on the derived grain representation

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into social practice has been accompanied by the emergence of new forms of unlawful conduct, requiring a reconsideration of traditional institutions of criminal law. The most challenging cases for criminal-law qualification arise where an AI system operates with partial or full autonomy, independently determining the means of achieving a goal set by a human. In such situations, establishing a causal link between the user’s conduct and the resulting socially dangerous consequences does not, in itself, constitute a sufficient basis for criminal liability, thereby raising the issue of the limits of subjective attribution. Based on the normative framework of the 2021 Criminal Code of the Republic of Armenia governing guilt, mistake as to factual circumstances, harm caused without guilt, and justified risk, the article argues that AI cannot be recognized as an independent subject of criminal liability. To determine the limits of criminal-law attribution, the author distinguishes three models of criminally relevant use of AI: the instrumental model (AI as a means of implementing criminal intent), the risk-based model (the use of AI in circumstances where the possibility of a socially dangerous consequence is foreseen or ought to be foreseen), and the autonomous-result model (the occurrence of a result that was not encompassed by the person’s intent and whose possibility the person was neither required nor able to foresee). The principle of controlled autonomy formulated in the article makes it possible to determine the boundary between culpable harm caused by a human and a result of the autonomous operation of an intelligent system that cannot be attributed to that person.

This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for using marketing analytics as a tool for strategic decision-making in advertising management in the context of sustainable development. The relevance of this study stems from the digital transformation of marketing activities, the growth in data volumes, the increasing complexity of consumer behavior models, and the need to shift from evaluating advertising activities primarily based on economic criteria to a comprehensive consideration of the economic, social, and environmental outcomes of advertising strategies. The role of marketing analytics as a component of the information and analytical support for strategic advertising management is substantiated; its functional purpose lies in transforming marketing data into relevant information for justifying, selecting, and adjusting strategic decisions. The functional purpose of descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics in the process of developing advertising strategies is revealed. The paper identifies opportunities for applying artificial intelligence, machine learning, and predictive modeling technologies to segment target audiences, personalize advertising messages, forecast consumer behavior, and optimize advertising investments. The paper justifies the need to integrate the principles of sustainable development into the system for evaluating the effectiveness of advertising strategies. It proposes a system of indicators structured around economic, social, and environmental components, which makes it possible to take into account – alongside the commercial effectiveness of advertising investments – brand trust, responsibility and transparency of advertising communications, the impact on the formation of sustainable consumption patterns, the environmental impact of advertising activities, and the risks of greenwashing. For a comprehensive assessment, an integral index of sustainable advertising strategy performance (ISRAS) is proposed, which involves aggregating normalized indicators of economic, social, and environmental performance and can be used for a multi-criteria comparison of alternative advertising strategies. To illustrate the ISRAS application algorithm, a demonstration calculation was performed using two hypothetical scenarios of IKEA’s advertising strategy and model normalized values. Scientific and practical recommendations have been formulated for improving the strategic decision-making process in advertising management based on an integrated analytical and strategic approach that encompasses analytical diagnosis, the formulation of strategic alternatives, their multi-criteria evaluation, the selection and implementation of an advertising strategy, monitoring, and strategic adjustments. The feasibility of transitioning from a piecemeal assessment of advertising campaign effectiveness to a comprehensive evaluation of the sustained effectiveness of advertising strategies has been substantiated. The potential for integrating marketing analytics and the principles of sustainable development has been identified to enhance the soundness of strategic advertising decisions, optimize marketing resources, strengthen consumer trust, minimize reputational and environmental risks, and create long-term value for the enterprise, consumers, and society.

ABSTRACT Generative AI systems are increasingly integrated into various user support and decision‐making contexts. While extensive research has explored user acceptance of generative AI across domains, less is known about how its inherent presentation features influence such acceptance. This study investigates how the presentation format of generative AI responses—high‐dynamism formats (word‐by‐word) versus low‐dynamism formats (line‐by‐line)—affects users' willingness to accept its output. Three experiments, across various contexts, including daily question‐answering, online shopping, and crowdfunding platforms, tested how the dynamic presentation of generative AI responses influences users' willingness to accept its output. The results demonstrate that users exhibit greater receptivity when generative AI responses are presented in high‐dynamism formats. This effect occurs because dynamic presentation enhances users' feelings of immersion. Furthermore, we find that users' situational need for understanding moderates this immersion‐based mechanism. Specifically, the positive indirect effect of dynamic presentation on willingness to accept the output through feelings of immersion is attenuated in high need‐for‐understanding contexts, where users tend to prioritize content quality, accuracy, and diagnosticity. In contrast, this indirect effect is amplified in low need‐for‐understanding contexts, where users are more receptive to the experiential and interactional qualities of dynamic presentation. This research contributes to the literature on the effectiveness of dynamic presentation and provides novel insights into the factors influencing user acceptance of generative AI outputs. Our findings highlight the importance of tailoring output presentation methods based on individual user characteristics and task‐specific cognitive demands.

The Boeing 737 MAX disasters killed 346 people and exposed profound failures involving aircraft design, automation, human-factors assumptions, corporate safety culture, and federal regulatory oversight. This article examines those failures against the emergence of a new flight-management-system software defect capable of disengaging vertical navigation (VNAV) during certain missed-approach sequences on affected 737 MAX aircraft. Rather than equating the VNAV issue with the catastrophic MCAS failures, the analysis considers a more fundamental question: whether Boeing and the Federal Aviation Administration have adequately incorporated the lessons of the MAX accidents when known automation deficiencies can still be mitigated through increased pilot workload while permanent engineering corrections remain pending. The investigation further examines Boeing’s criminal-accountability history, including the federal fraud charge, deferred prosecution agreement, subsequent determination that Boeing breached that agreement, proposed guilty plea, and eventual non-prosecution agreement. Particular attention is given to Boeing’s extensive political presence, campaign and inaugural contributions, federal lobbying, regulatory relationships, and its selection for major next-generation U.S. fighter programs. No evidence examined establishes a quid pro quo between Boeing’s political activities, prosecutorial outcomes, or defense contracts; however, the record reveals substantial structural interdependence between Boeing and the federal institutions responsible for regulating, prosecuting, and purchasing from the company. The article argues that after 346 deaths, reliance upon pilots to compensate procedurally for correctable automation deficiencies deserves exceptional scrutiny and that Boeing’s strategic importance should not insulate the corporation or its decision-makers from meaningful regulatory and criminal accountability.

3D concrete printing (3DCP) has revolutionized the construction industry, allowing for the produc-tion of complex geometries with greater efficiency and sustainability. This is despite ongoing challenges with structural reliability and long-term performance, which are due to the material's anisotropic properties and layer interfaces.This study performed a bibliometric analysis of the literature on the structural analysis of 3DCP, using VOSviewer to identify research trends and gaps. The methodology included a keyword search in the Scopus database, which resulted in 108 selected articles after a rigorous screening process. The results in-dicate a significant increase in 3DCP research since 2018, with a projected peak of 40 articles published in 2025. A co-occurrence analysis of keywords revealed a concentration on "concretes," "concrete printings," and "finite element method," highlighting research into material failure and behavior. The 108 works, au-thored by 374 individuals, were distributed across 8 clusters, with 23 papers showing co-authorship. Maximil-iano Cremonesi, Liberato Ferrara, and Giacomo Rizzieri had the strongest collaborations between 2024 and 2025. China and the United States lead in publications, with 37 and 12 articles, respectively, and China also leads in collaborations with 14. The Journal of Building Engineering was the most relevant journal, with 11 publications. Despite these advancements, the study points to significant gaps, such as the need for more so-phisticated numerical models to simulate interlayer and multi-scale interactions. The integration of structural reinforcements and a better understanding of the long-term durability of 3DCP are also critical challenges. Furthermore, there is a major opportunity for research in multifunctional materials and the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning to optimize design and predict performance, thereby boosting sus-tainability in 3DCP.

Abstract The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has generated profound philosophical questions concerning intelligence, agency, autonomy, responsibility, human values, technological power, and the future of humanity. Among contemporary philosophers, Nick Bostrom has provided one of the most systematic philosophical analyses of the long-term risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence. His conception of the problem is principally concerned with the possibility that artificial general intelligence may develop into superintelligence whose cognitive and strategic capacities surpass those of human beings. The central difficulty, according to Bostrom, is not merely whether machines can think, but whether humanity can retain meaningful control over machines that may eventually become more intelligent and strategically capable than their creators. This article critically examined Bostrom's conception of the problem of artificial intelligence, focusing on his notions of superintelligence, existential risk, the orthogonality thesis, instrumental convergence, and the control problem. It argued that Bostrom's analysis provides an important conceptual foundation for contemporary debates on artificial intelligence safety and alignment but requires philosophical supplementation when considered from an African perspective. In particular, the individualistic assumptions that can underlie some formulations of artificial intelligence ethics require enrichment through African conceptions of communal responsibility, relational personhood, human dignity, and social embeddedness. The article concluded that Bostrom's conception of artificial intelligence is philosophically valuable as a theory of technological control and existential risk, but its relevance to Africa is strengthened when integrated with relational and communitarian conceptions of personhood and responsibility. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Nick Bostrom, superintelligence, existential risk, alignment, control problem, African philosophy.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in landscape architecture to accelerate design development and enhance stakeholder engagement. This study presents a new landscape concept design tool to support collaborative greenspace problem-solving by integrating rapid scenario generation with a Pollinator Habitat Indicator (PHI). We define this as the PHI-AI Landscape Design Tool. The model combines text-to-image generative workflows with a simplified pollinator-oriented reference that compares AI-generated scenarios based on broad landscape cover composition. The PHI-AI Landscape Design Tool generated varied concept layouts with planting and pathway configurations responsive to descriptive prompts and user-defined parameters. It generates layout variations that reflect visually coherent planting configurations, and circulation connections to existing infrastructure for user functionality. This enables the rapid production of multiple design alternatives that remain legible, adaptable, and flexible to human-controlled editing prompts for stakeholder engagement. This study offers a framework for integrating a simplified ecological reference into the planning phase of landscape design.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are increasingly deployed within higher education to support admissions decision-making, student success initiatives, and personalised learning. However, most AI-enabled admissions systems remain narrowly focused on efficiency, prediction, and institutional optimisation, with limited attention to learner agency, educational equity, transparency, and human-centred support. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than merely a selection or gatekeeping process. The study adopts a conceptual and integrative literature review approach, synthesising scholarship from human-centred artificial intelligence, learning analytics, personalised learning, educational equity, explainable AI, generative AI, responsible AI governance, learner agency theory, and value-sensitive design. To strengthen transparency during revision, the integrative synthesis was supplemented by a targeted ERIC search and bibliographic verification using publisher and authoritative policy repositories. Drawing upon these interdisciplinary perspectives, the paper develops the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF), a governance-oriented model for ethical and transparent AI adoption in higher education admissions and enrolment management. The framework comprises five interconnected dimensions: learner profiling and contextual understanding; explainable AI decision support; equity and inclusion auditing; human oversight and shared decision-making; and personalised transition and success support. Together, these dimensions provide a governance architecture for evaluating how admissions might be connected to personalised educational pathways while making explicit the trade-offs among equity, privacy, explainability, accuracy, human oversight, and learner agency. The framework identifies governance mechanisms required to address algorithmic bias, transparency, privacy, accountability, and learner autonomy. A five-stage Human-Centred AI Ecosystem extending governance across the full student lifecycle — from admissions through to graduate development — provides a further organising contribution. The study advances existing literature by integrating admissions analytics, learning analytics, personalised learning, learner agency, and responsible AI governance within a unified framework. Unlike conventional admissions models that prioritise institutional efficiency, HCPAF positions admissions as the foundation of a personalised learning ecosystem and conceptualises trust as a relational, calibrated, and empirically contingent construct connecting transparency, fairness, learner agency, and AI adoption. The framework contributes to emerging debates concerning ethical and human-centred AI in education and identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4, 10, and 16, while emphasising that any contribution to those goals requires empirical validation. Introduces the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF) for equitable and personalised higher education enrolment. Repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than a terminal selection mechanism. Integrates human-centred AI, learning analytics, educational equity, explainable AI, learner agency, and responsible governance. Introduces trust as a central mediating construct linking transparency, fairness, and AI adoption in education. Provides a governance roadmap for ethical, transparent, and accountable AI adoption across the student lifecycle. Identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4 (Quality Education), 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions), subject to empirical validation. Establishes a multi-dimensional research agenda for human-centred AI in higher education.

Scout Moor II (12 turbines up to 180 m to blade tip, Rossendale and Rochdale, applications 2025/0267 and 25/00680/FUL) and Calderdale Energy Park (34 turbines in its April 2026 preliminary environmental information report) are proposed on the South Pennines with their nearest turbines 15.7 km apart. The paper builds a cumulative zone of theoretical visibility for the two schemes entirely from open data (OS Terrain 50 at 50 m, eye 2 m, refraction coefficient 0.075, 45 km from each turbine, a single blade tip counts) and checks it against the applicants' own figures and software. On bare earth, 698.9 km² of land sees at least one turbine of each scheme; the applicant's own QGIS plugin, given the same inputs, gives 685.4 km², and one sight line per cell gives 664.4 km². Where both models compute, the applicant's own combined map (Further Environmental Information Figure 11.16) agrees with the model (intersection over union 0.88). The paper then tests what screening does. On the Environment Agency's first-return LIDAR surface, the combined view is lost at 49 of the 51 highest-scoring settlement points at the point itself, and kept at 17 on a small grid of observers around the point (12 counting only observers within 100 m). On the applicant's own screening rule, rebuilt from the notes on its Figures 11.7 and 11.8 with the observer on the ground, 174.9 km² of the 206.7 km² of its "both may be visible" class within 20 km keeps the view, and 35 of the 62 settlement points in that class. What went against the author is reported in the main text: the cell rule, the ground-level rule, a re-sited viewpoint, the screening results, the roof-observer error found by a hostile read, the errors of the first-round objection and their correction, and four errors of wording in the round-two documents, one of them corrected on the site. The deposit contains the paper (Markdown), the model and its tests, every model output, the representation and articles as sent or published, the audit, review and method records, and a source manifest citing every applicant document by URL and SHA-256 rather than copying it. reproduce.py checks the inputs, can rebuild every grid from the open data in three tiers, and recomputes 408 figures, some a second way; tools/check_paper.py checks every model figure quoted in the paper, the representation, its appendices and the article against that output. Run "uv run python reproduce.py", then "uv run python tools/check_paper.py". The author objected to the Scout Moor II applications in a personal capacity and as county councillor for Padiham and Burnley West, Lancashire County Council, and is the council's Cabinet Member for Adult Social Care; see the Declaration of Interests. The applications are live; the paper describes a method and its checks and takes no position on the decision. Autonomous mobile robots that coexist with humans must construct not only geometric maps but also semantic maps that can be accessed through natural language. Conventional semantic mapping has mainly focused on assigning labels from predefined closed vocabularies to metric maps, limiting its ability to handle novel objects, open-ended linguistic expressions, and flexible human-robot interaction. Recent advances in large-scale foundation models, particularly LLMs and VLMs, have accelerated research on open-vocabulary semantic mapping. In parallel, generative 3D representations such as neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splatting have enabled dense, continuous spatial representations associated with language-derived features. Together, these developments allow robots to acquire spatial semantic representations that connect perception, language, and action. This paper reviews this rapidly evolving field through a four-part taxonomy: (i) fusion of semantic features into 3D metric maps; (ii) object-centric open-vocabulary representations; (iii) hierarchical scene graph representations; and (iv) continuous generative 3D language fields. We also revisit the history of open-vocabulary semantic mapping and provide an overview of foundation model-based navigation using language-accessible maps, ranging from object-goal navigation to LLM-based hierarchical task planning. Finally, we introduce evaluation datasets, simulators, robot platforms, and evaluation metrics, and summarize seven open challenges.

In recent years, Computer Vision (CV) has evolved rapidly, enabling enhanced automation, safety, inspection, and logistics across manufacturing, construction, and robotics. This systematic review surveys current computer vision applications in industrial environments, spanning factory defect inspection, construction-site safety, warehouse inventory tracking, and industrial robotics. From more than 8,700 initially identified studies, we selected 146 key papers representing cross-domain CV applications. The survey is organized into four thematic areas: visual inspection and defect detection, worker safety and monitoring, inventory and logistics tracking, and robotics and automation. For each area, we compare state-of-the-art approaches, datasets, and deployment settings while highlighting the factors that influence their performance under different operating conditions. For example, YOLO-based detectors dominate real-time edge deployment because of their high throughput, whereas transformer-based models often struggle to scale in resource-constrained environments despite their superior feature extraction capabilities. We also identify critical research gaps. Although manufacturing and construction benefit from numerous public datasets for quality inspection and safety monitoring, warehousing and robotics continue to lack large-scale, real-world benchmark datasets. Finally, we discuss emerging research directions, including domain adaptation, edge AI, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), to support the development of more robust, scalable, and balanced computer vision solutions for industrial applications.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly evolving from systems that generate recommendations and content towards autonomous agents capable of planning, reasoning, interacting with external systems, using tools and executing actions with limited human intervention. As AI systems become more agentic, accountability can no longer be understood solely as a legal obligation or post-incident governance exercise. It must also become an operational property embedded into the design, deployment and operation of autonomous AI systems. ACAAI (Accountability by Design for Agentic AI) approaches accountability as a systems engineering property that emerges from the coordinated implementation of organizational and technical controls rather than from any single governance mechanism. Building upon principles from AI governance, cybersecurity, safety engineering, resilience engineering and AI assurance, the framework translates existing governance principles into more than 100 organizational and technical controls spanning the lifecycle of agentic AI systems. ACAAI is structured around six complementary control domains: (1) Organizational Governance, (2) Human Oversight, Consent and Decision Authority, (3) Identity, Authority and Data Governance, (4) Observability, Explainability and Evidence, (5) Runtime Safety and Assurance, and (6) Incident Response and Recovery. Rather than proposing a new regulatory model or prescriptive implementation methodology, ACAAI provides a structured engineering foundation for designing, deploying, operating and retiring accountable autonomous AI systems. The framework also dentifies research and implementation challenges that remain as agentic AI systems become increasingly autonomous, interconnected and collaborative.

documents.abstract: An empirical, runtime-verified study of the 'execution control plane' layer of the AI-agent ecosystem: services named agent-exec-gateway, agent-sandbox, code-sandbox, or policy engine that are supposed to constrain agent execution by policy, approval, and isolation. Scanning ~500 freshly-published MCP/A2A/agent repositories across five attack-surface dimensions (supply-chain poisoning, permission-escaping, credential storage, prompt-injection defense, protocol implementation), we confirm and responsibly disclose 4 exploitable vulnerabilities whose shared root cause is 'control-plane trust inversion': the component named for restriction ships as an unauthenticated, direct code-execution endpoint (CWE-306), enabling policy bypass and arbitrary command/Python execution with output read-back. A control group of seven hardened implementations (fail-closed boot, constant-time HMAC compare, single-use approval, gvisor/VM isolation) shows the ecosystem is two-sided: established agent infrastructure is hardened while freshly-published 0-star 'control-plane' repositories repeatedly invert the trust model. We provide detection signatures, honest deployment-boundary analysis (loopback vs 0.0.0.0 Docker), and hardening guidance.

Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) refers to a kind of artificial intelligence that is able to learn, reason, and perform a wide range of intellectual tasks at the same or better levels as humans do. This paper explores the implications that AGI might have on humanity if it was to become a reality, especially its effects on work, society, and human dependency on intelligent machines. However, the scope of the discussion does not focus on whether AGI would replace human labor, but rather on whether humans would be less central to the organization of society.

As artificial intelligence advances at an unprecedented pace, the conversation surrounding its potential to destroy humanity often revolves around science fiction scenarios, rogue machines, and autonomous weapons. But what if the greatest threat isn't AI turning against us, but a world that becomes so dependent on it that we can no longer function without it? In AI and the "End of the World," Simon Abayomi Olawuyi explores a hypothetical future where AI permeates every aspect of human existence, from critical infrastructure and personal identity to employment, information, and the very concept of truth. Through a speculative look at the road from the 2022 AI boom to 2035, the piece examines a different kind of existential risk: a society so deeply intertwined with artificial intelligence that disconnecting from it could become more dangerous than keeping it running.

The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday work has made employees' ability to understand, evaluate and collaborate with AI systems a strategic human resource. This paper asks how employees' AI literacy relates to their readiness for the future skills that employers increasingly demand, and how AI self-efficacy and organisational training support shape that relationship. The study proceeds in two phases. Study 1 synthesises published workforce evidence from the World Economic Forum (2025), Microsoft and LinkedIn (2024), the OECD (2024) and the Federal Reserve (2024, 2025), documenting a structural 'demand-readiness gap' in which demand for AI-fluent employees outpaces structured training provision. analyses an illustrative, calibrated employee dataset (N = 384) using measurement validation, hierarchical regression, bootstrapped mediation and moderation analysis. AI literacy was positively associated with future skills readiness (beta = 0.70, p < .001), and AI self-efficacy partially mediated this association (indirect effect = 0.13, 95% bootstrap CI [0.08, 0.18]). Organisational training support strengthened the literacy-readiness association (interaction beta = 0.18, p < .001), such that the relationship was significant under high support but weaker under low support. Human-AI collaboration and critical evaluation emerged as the strongest literacy dimensions, and readiness differed significantly across job functions. The study positions AI literacy as organisationally contingent human capital and proposes a training-architecture framework for HRM. Findings are directional and should be read in light of the simulated nature of the dataset.

Organisational training support strengthened the literacy-readiness association (interaction beta = 0.18, p < .001), such that the relationship was significant under high support but weaker under low support. Human-AI collaboration and critical evaluation emerged as the strongest literacy dimensions, and readiness differed significantly across job functions. The study positions AI literacy as organisationally contingent human capital and proposes a training-architecture framework for HRM. Findings are directional and should be read in light of the simulated nature of the dataset.

Generative AI complicates translation evaluation because fluent outputs may introduce unsupported meaning, while non-literal renderings may represent legitimate interpretation. This study examined Vietnamese EFL students’ evaluation of AI-generated translations and its associations with digital competence, translation competence, and critical-evaluation confidence. A cross-sectional study involved 213 final-year English majors who completed a 25-item performance task and self-report scales. Students were considerably more accurate in recognising problematic outputs than in diagnosing their type (68.0% vs. 38.4%). Critical-evaluation confidence showed the strongest association with performance (r=.85), although its conceptual overlap with the performance task warrants caution. In the full regression model, translation competence (β=.31) and digital competence (β=.16) contributed significantly alongside critical-evaluation confidence (β=.64), whereas AI-use frequency did not. When the overlapping critical-evaluation measure was removed, the model still explained 55% of performance variance, with translation competence showing the strongest association (β=.61). The findings indicate that evaluating AI-generated translation depends less on frequency of AI use than on students’ translation knowledge and evaluative judgement, particularly their ability to distinguish unsupported generation from defensible interpretation. Rather than simply as a translation tool Generative AI should thus be used as an object of critical inquiry. Alternative AI renderings may expose students to interpretations they had not considered, including potentially productive expansions of source meaning. This approach preserves the interpretive character of translation while making students accountable for the decisions they ultimately accept.

The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) art generators has introduced algorithmically created paintings into mainstream consumer markets, yet consumers consistently assign lower value to AI-generated works than to human-created equivalents. This paper proposes perceived creative authenticity---consumers' subjective perception that an artwork reflects a genuine creative process characterized by human-centered values of originality, craftsmanship, and uniqueness---as a theoretically distinct mechanism explaining this value differential. Conceptually differentiated from perceived creativity, which concerns the novelty of the artistic output, perceived creative authenticity addresses the genuineness of the creator-work relationship. Drawing on authenticity theory and Psychological Ownership Theory, we develop a moderated mediation framework hypothesizing that (H1) human authorship elicits higher perceived value than AI authorship, (H2) perceived creative authenticity mediates this effect, while the indirect effects through perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs are not significant, establishing perceived creative authenticity as the primary explanatory mechanism within the tested model, and (H3) non-fungible token (NFT) authentication attenuates the mediated pathway by providing verifiable creative provenance. Across five studies, results support this framework: Study 1 conceptually replicates the human-AI value gap among Chinese consumers; Studies 2a—2c demonstrate the mediating role of perceived creative authenticity: Study 2a establishes the basic mediation pathway; Study 2b shows through parallel mediation that perceived creative authenticity uniquely mediates the effect while perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs do not exhibit significant indirect effects; and Study 2c provides causal evidence through a moderation-of-process design; and Study 3 shows that NFT authentication narrows the authenticity gap between human and AI art. These findings advance the literature on human-computer interaction by identifying process-based authenticity judgments as a key psychological mechanism shaping consumer responses to algorithmic creative products, with implications for artists and platforms navigating digital art markets.

documents.abstract: Volunteer organizations play a critical role in civil society, yet many face increasing difficulty finding, developing, and replacing volunteer leaders. Demographic change, evolving patterns of civic participation, competing demands on volunteers’ time, and volunteer fatigue create significant challenges for leadership continuity. Although succession planning has been extensively studied in corporate and professional contexts, less attention has been given to volunteer organizations, where authority, engagement, and leadership development operate differently.This article examines succession challenges in volunteer organizations and argues that succession planning should be understood as an ongoing responsibility of governance and stewardship rather than a response to leadership vacancies. Drawing on literature concerning succession planning, nonprofit leadership, volunteer management, social capital, and civic engagement, the article proposes an actionable six-step model emphasizing leadership commitment, role clarity, succession-risk assessment, identification and development of potential successors, and redesign of leadership roles to strengthen continuity and leadership pipelines. A hypothetical community arts organization illustrates the model’s practical application.The article further examines how artificial intelligence can augment succession planning in resource-constrained volunteer organizations through knowledge capture, role clarification, leadership development, and continuity planning. AI is conceptualized as a capacity-building tool rather than a substitute for human judgment. Volunteer leaders remain responsible for organizational context, confidentiality, fairness, governance, and succession decisions. The resulting approach positions AI-augmented succession planning as a human-centered strategy for strengthening leadership continuity, institutional knowledge, and organizational resilience.

Abstract Cloud-based systems demand secure yet efficient file access mechanisms. Traditional encryption frameworks often introduce latency and resource overhead, limiting scalability. Building on Astillero's (2026) AI-driven logic gate synthesis, this paper explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can optimize encrypted file access. By applying Reinforcement Learning (RL), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and Large Circuit Models (LCMs), AI enables adaptive encryption, predictive access control, and efficient resource allocation. This study also integrates recent research on AI-based workload management and reinforcement learning for secure access control, highlighting how intelligent systems can balance security, scalability, and performance.

This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance employee retention amidst significant turnover issues in modern organizations. It conducts a systematic review of 58 sources, including peer-reviewed articles and practitioner reports, predominantly from 2015 to 2026, and proposes an integrative conceptual framework. The findings indicate a discrepancy between improved predictive accuracy for voluntary turnover and inconsistent retention gains, particularly in organizations with advanced analytics capabilities. Resistance from employees often stems from concerns about fairness, transparency, and surveillance. The study introduces a dual-pathway model: the enabling pathway, where analytics lead to interventions that enhance job embeddedness and retention, and the evaluative pathway, where perceptions of justice and privacy can undermine these benefits. The paper advances nine propositions detailing these relationships and uniquely integrates four existing research areas—HR analytics, algorithmic management, organizational justice, and turnover theory—reconceptualizing retention analytics as a matter of decision quality and legitimacy rather than mere predictive accuracy. It lays out a research agenda for future empirical inquiries and offers practical recommendations for ethical AI deployment in HR decision-making.
